speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: S.S. "EMPEROR" STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT ON STRANDING AND SINKING OF VESSEL IN LAKE SUPERIOR ON JUNE 4
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Transport to the S.S. Emperor disaster on lake Superior the day before yesterday and to ask what action has been
Privilege-Mr. Low

taken to have an inquiry held by the wreck commissioner. I refer the minister to what has appeared in the press of yesterday and today from Port Arthur. There are no aids to navigation or life-saving stations on the great lakes. In 1928 I brought up in the house the necessity of providing aids to navigation and life-saving stations for the protection of life on the great lakes. We have to rely on United States life-saving stations, as in the disaster to Canadian seamen on this lake in 1928. I should like to know what action is being taken.

subtopic: S.S. "EMPEROR" STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT ON STRANDING AND SINKING OF VESSEL IN LAKE SUPERIOR ON JUNE 4
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know
whether the hon. gentleman has read the report of the accident, but if he had I am sure he would not have asked that question, at least not phrased in the manner in which it was. I expected that one such question would be asked today and I have prepared a statement.
The S.S. Emperor left Port Arthur about 11.30 p.m. on June 3, eastward bound, loaded with ore. In the early hours of the morning of the 4th, at approximately five o'clock she struck Canoe rocks, a submerged rock reef three and a half miles west of Blake Point light, Isle Royale, lake Superior, and broke in two.
According to the information at present available, two boats were lowered, one of which was swamped when the steamer went down.
The United States lighthouse tender Kimball, which was in the vicinity, received the distress signal from the Emperor at 5.15 a.m. and arrived at the scene of the casualty at 5.50 a.m., or about thirty-five minutes after the distress signal was picked up. Though exact information as to weather visibility at the time is not yet available, it is understood that the weather was good, and that the sea was comparatively smooth. The Kimball rescued twenty-one survivors and recovered the body of a woman. They were taken into Fort William. A further search was made and another woman's body was found and landed at Fort William by the Kimball on the night of Wednesday, the 4th instant. In addition to a thorough search of the area by the Kimball and two other small vessels of the United States lighthouse service, a coast guard plane made a thorough search of the area but no further survivors or bodies have been found.
Captain W. N. Morrison, Examiner Masters and Mates, of this department, is in Port Arthur at the moment holding a preliminary inquiry into the casualty.

subtopic: CROP FAILURE PAYMENTS-AWARDS TO FARMERS WITH MINIMUM PRODUCTION

speechtext: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 261, to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, 1939.

subtopic: CROP FAILURE PAYMENTS-AWARDS TO FARMERS WITH MINIMUM PRODUCTION
speechtext:
I desire to offer a few comments on this bill at this stage. It is significant, Mr. Speaker, that there was called in the year 1938 what was known throughout this nation as the Bracken wheat conference in Winnipeg. At that time they recommended an initial price of not less than eighty cents a bushel. In those days market conditions were difficult in the Dominion of Canada. Following that, there was the original plan by the federal government to drop the initial price to sixty cents a bushel and pay an acreage bonus on yields up to fifteen bushels an acre. However, the final policy of the government of the day was to pay seventy cents initial payment and acreage bonus up to

a yield of twelve bushels an acre. The act was brought into being in 1939 on that basis.
The application of the act applied and still applies to all three prairie provinces and the Peace River block in British Columbia. There are three main sections in the act. There was the national emergency section which provided that in any year the price of wheat was less than eighty cents a bushel the minister could declare it an emergency year. Each farmer residing in a township with the following average yields was to receive the following awards: up to four bushels and under, $2 an acre on half the cultivated acreage; from four to eight bushels an acre, $1.50 an acre on half the cultivated acreage; from eight to ten bushels an acre, $1 per acre with a limit of 200 acres on which he could receive an award. This section was later amended so that the minister could declare an emergency year, regardless of the price that was being paid for wheat.
Section 4 dealt with crop failures. Regardless of the price of wheat, a province could be declared a crop failure area under the following conditions: at least ten townships with five bushels per acre or less in Alberta and Manitoba; in Saskatchewan at least 135 townships; awards: up to five bushels, $2.50 an acre on half the cultivated acreage and a maximum of $5.00 and a minimum of $2.00.
Section 6 provided for one per cent levy on all grains marketed in the prairie provinces, and that continues today. All farmers, including tenants actually farming the land, were eligible; ranchers were excluded and businessmen doing part-time farming were also excluded. Farmers who had more than 3,000 bushels and more than eight bushels per acre are ineligible. Otherwise all farmers receive the bonus, regardless of their yield if they are in an eligible township.
A recent amendment excludes from an eligible township any block of nine sections which has an average yield of more than ten bushels per acre, if the block lies next to an ineligible township. The same amendment brings into the eligible class any block of nine sections with an average yield of ten bushels per acre or less in an ineligible township if it lies contiguous to an eligible township, and that has been our difficulty from the point of administration.
With respect to administration, the head office has been located in Regina with branch offices in Edmonton for Alberta and in Winnipeg for Manitoba. The township yields are obtained by inspectors appointed for that purpose who make personal calls and obtain

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
the production and -acreage of each farmer, within these areas, I believe, after application has been made by the municipal officials asking that it be done. The superintendent then presents all the township data to the board of review which passes on the eligibility of the township.
The operation of the act from 1939 to 1946 inclusive has brought in, under this one per cent levy, the following receipts:	from
Alberta, $6,205,000; from Manitoba, $3,619,000, and from Saskatchewan, $12,895,000. The payments made within the provinces are as follows: for Alberta, $15,209,000; for Manitoba, $1,730,000, and for Saskatchewan, $45,558,000. The total levy collected under that scheme has been $22,719,000, while total payments have amounted to $62,497,000. In addition, there have been administration costs, amounting, on the average, to about $300,000 a year.
Several of us have put questions on the order paper and received answers by way of returns, and we find that for seven years in succession eighty-two of these townships have received these P.F.A.A. payments; 396 townships have received these payments for six consecutive years; 849 townships have received them for five years in succession, and 1,383 townships have received the payments in four consecutive years. The act has been in force for eight years, and in only one year, 1942, were no payments made.
On previous occasions I have referred to the fact that at times the operation of this act is somewhat in contradiction to the operation of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. What it means, as I think can be readily proved by the fact that some of these farmers have received payments for seven years hand running, is that many of these people are farming sub-marginal land. Enough money has already been paid out in this way to purchase the land. Approximately 1,160 farmers who received the bonus for seven years were paid a total of $2 million. Based on the 1946 cultivated acreage, after ten years the farmers received $5 per acre for their land, or a total of about $1,760 each. In some townships the average total amount paid would be approximately $7 per acre. I know of land in my own constituency, in the Palliser triangle, owned by one of the municipalities for grazing purposes, which I am sorry to say they are not continuing to hold for that purpose, which now is being sold to operators for $2 an acre. Quite frankly, this is land which I do not believe should be put under the plough. So I think it will be seen that this matter calls for quite a bit of serious consideration.
I have a great deal of detail here. I do not want to discuss the matter at least at this time because, as I said at the resolution stage, we have an undertaking from the minister that the bill is to go to the agriculture committee, where I am sure it will receive close scrutiny.' I do say, however, that this act should have only one clause dealing with eligibility, instead of two; that is, the crop failure and the emergency year. In the second place, it should be on an individual basis, not on a township basis. The part township clause and section 8 have not solved the problem so far. The act should provide that the land of any farmer who becomes eligible for these payments during seven successive years would be purchased by the government for community pastures under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. It is a waste of public money to keep the act functioning as it is at present, and probably have operators living under conditions under which they should not attempt to farm. There is some argument as to whether the territory within those provinces should be zoned and some smaller categories provided. In some cases the payments should be larger. However I seriously urge the government to consider the possibility, after so many successive crop failures, of purchasing that land for community pastures.
As I have said, there are many more things which might be discussed, but since we are going to take up these matters in the committee on agriculture, I think I should reserve much of my comment for that stage.

Before the bill passes, I should like to say a word or two concerning it. The present Prairie Farm Assistance Act is a definite improvement over the act which it replaces. As I understand it, the payments may be made any year without the necessity of a declaration of an emergency year. That is all to the good. But the payment may now be made only on the basis of nine sections, as I gather it, provided that those nine sections are adjacent to a township which is declared eligible. While that is much better than it was formerly, it is not yet as it should be. We social crediters believe that there should be a crop insurance scheme across Canada, and that losses ought to be paid on an individual basis rather than on the basis of a number of sections or townships.
It may be argued, Mr. Speaker, that constitutionally the federal government could not pass an act for such a scheme of universal insurance for farmers. We do not sympathize with that point of view. We believe that the federal government could take care of crop insurance by passing enabling legislation much as is done in the case of old age pensions, permitting the money to be provided to the provinces, allowing each province to come in with its own legislation providing for crop insurance within the province, and allowing each province also to take over in large measure the administration of the act. In the 83166-244i
days to come this sort of arrangement ought to be made by the dominion government and will be recognized everywhere as being the sound, most effective and economical way of taking care of this important matter.
It will be urged that the dominion government could not possibly supply the funds necessary for a universal crop insurance scheme. On the face of existing realities, such a contention does not quite make sense. Undoubtedly in this country we are able to produce enough goods and services of all kinds to provide all the farmers in Canada with an adequate income in any given year, regardless of whether they are hailed, rained out, frozen out or in any other way deprived of their crops. Approaching the matter from that common sense, realistic point of view, I think every member in the house and everyone throughout the country will grant that it simply is not quite reasonable that we should be without a crop insurance scheme from coast to coast in Canada, covering every kind of agricultural endeavour. If Canada is able to produce sufficient goods and services to provide for the needs of her population, agricultural and non-agricultural, up to a given standard of living, that fact indicates quite clearly that the national credit could be used as a means of providing the money with which to buy crop insurance.
The minister deserves commendation for the steps which he has taken thus far in the development of this Prairie Farm Assistance Act. He has gone a long way since the inception of the scheme. He is making progress surely and probably as rapidly as public opinion will permit him to do at the present time; he is showing unmistakable signs of a progressive attitude in this matter. We social crediters desire to commend him for his past efforts and to congratulate him on the measure which he is now introducing. We shall follow it through with great interest and with complete readiness to support him in all forwardlooking steps.

We have to advise again that the prairie farm assistance payments are made on a township basis. That is, a township -must be declared eligible by the board of review before this department can make payment, and in order for the board -to qualify such township for payment, they must find the average yield of wheat to be less than 8 bushels per acre. There is only one exception to the township being a unit for payment and that is, when an ineligible -township, -and the board find 9 or more sections forming a rectangular block, having an average yield of wheat of 8 or less bushels per acre and the side of this block of sections bordering an eligible township, the board may then qualify such a block of sections for payment under section 7 (b) of the act.

In so far as township 51-16 With is concerned, the average yield of wheat for -the township was found to be considerably in excess of 8 bushels per acre. Mr. Speaker, since we have the assurance of the minister that the bill is to go before the agriculture committee I shall be brief. However, as I am not a member of that committee I have a few suggestions I should like to offer at this time. First, I should like to commend the minister for the changes provided by the bill, but in my view there are many more changes that should be made if we are to give the farmers the real protection they have been looking for in the past few years.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

The difference in soil and climatic conditions in the various parts of Saskatchewan are manifold. In the south we have drought conditions, but drought in the northern areas is quite uncommon. On the other hand, the northern areas of the province are subject to frost damage and damage from insect infestation. All through the province we have the menace from hail. The losses from drought in the south are much greater than the crop losses in the north caused by frost or other adverse conditions. Both in the northern and southern areas the differences in soil have a considerable bearing upon the losses sustained by individual farmers.
I believe I suggested last year that there should be a system of zoning in the provinces into crop risk areas with lower percentages of deduction in the low risk areas and higher percentages in the heavy risk districts. I believe that would make the burden of crop failure assistance much more equitable. A number of farm organizations have suggested this plan, so I am not the originator of it. At this time I should like to place on record a resolution passed by one of these organizations, the rural municipality of Weyburn, as recently as March 11, and I quote:
Resolved that deductions and payments during short crop years are too small and we recommend that the one per cent deduction for P.F.A.A. be increased in the southern part of the province with corresponding higher payments in crop failure areas.
The resolution goes on to favour zoning of the province to apportion the deductions and benefits. Reference is also made to the high protein wheat produced in the south. This may not be apropos of the question, but, since the minister no doubt has heard of it before, I think it would be wise for me to mention it. The recommendation is made that wheat from the south should be graded on a protein basis to give a premium on wheat grown in the dry area which would more than offset the higher deductions which zoning would require from the southern area.
In my opinion payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act- should be based on the individual farm yield. Several hon. members have expressed the same opinion. The present act provides for assistance to the farmer on the basis of the average yield of the township in which he resides. Even with the present changes allowing for a nine-section block, there is still a considerable amount of dissatisfaction. If it is not feasible to have - benefits on an individual farm basis I would suggest that the proposed rectangular block of nine sections be reduced to a smaller area. The present system seems to me unsatisfactory

because farmers living in the bonus area frequently, not only last year but in previous years, had substantial yields, but because they resided in a government "declared" area they were recipients of benefits under the act, while, on the other hand, farmers living on the fringe of the stricken area who had little or no crop at all received no benefits, since the average yield in the block in which they lived exceeded the maximum set by the act. Very often a farmer who failed to obtain the bonus lived just across the road from a neighbour who had received benefits under the act and had had a crop.
The act now reads that if a township has not the requisite yield to bring it within the act a rectangular block of not more than nine sections may be brought in. That is a good feature of the act. But this block of nine sections must be lying alongside an eligible township. This act should be amended to make it more flexible so that it would not be necessary to have a rectangular block, or to have it contiguous to an eligible township. Despite any changes which might be made in this particular regard, I am of the firm belief that benefits should be paid on an individual farm basis. There seems to be a sufficient number of inspectors now employed by the Department of Agriculture under this act to conduct the field work in this connection, so that no further operating expenses would be entailed. The farms in the stricken area have to be inspected anyway to ascertain the true situation in the stricken districts. I believe that this change in the act would actually save the government money, because many farmers now receive benefits under the act who are not in great need of those benefits. In any event, it seems to me that hail damage is nearly always on an individual farm basis. Certainly the damage runs in strips, so that damage at least from this source should be treated on an individual farm basis.
The act as it stands limits benefits paid to an individual farmer to a maximum of $400 or $500, depending upon whether the year is declared an "emergency year" or a "crop failure year". This is an inadequate provision and does not meet the farmers' needs. I think at this time I should draw the minister's attention to a resolution that was passed in convention last year by the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities. The minister is, I believe, quite familiar with the resolution, but I wish to place it on the record because it is well worthy of consideration. The resolution asks:

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
. . . that the crop failure bonus be increased to $5 per acre and that the maximum be $1,000, and the assessment 2 per cent, and that payments be made on an individual plan.
While the two per cent assessment might not be acceptable to areas in the north of the province where crop failure is less common, certainly it would be welcomed in the south if benefits under the act were increased. Zoning as previously suggested, to apportion the deductions and benefits would, I believe, be acceptable to all areas in the province.
Under present conditions where the yield is less than five bushels to the acre, a $1 payment is made per cultivated area, with a maximum of $400 per farmer, regardless of the acreage involved. That, in my opinion, is hardly adequate relief. Costs of farm operation have substantially increased. The purchase of the seed which would be necessary for the next crop year would, at present prices, cost the average farmer of 320 acres more than the benefits paid out now under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. The farmer also has food and clothing to purchase for his family and many other expenses as well. The maximum to be paid under the act should, I firmly believe, be increased to $1,000, which, with present high production costs, is certainly little enough.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that farmers in the west on the whole are thankful that there is such a thing as the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. It gives them a measure of security. It keeps the wolf from the door when crop failure is complete. But the wolf is never far away, because of the meagre benefits provided under the act.
I consider that the recommendations I have made deserve consideration. That is the reason I make them this afternoon, in order that they may be considered by the minister when this bill goes before the committee. I am sure that if they were incorporated in the bill it would make the act more effective and would establish a feeling of security for farmers everywhere in the western provinces. I am satisfied that the farmer is willing to contribute more to the fund if his benefits are to be on a more adequate scale. Finally, I believe that the zoning system is the only way to take care of inequalities, not only in the deductions scheme, but also in the benefits paid out under the act.

Mr. Speaker, the discussion that has taken place on the second reading of the bill has been not only interesting but quite instructive. I appreciate the remarks which have been made in. favour of the legislation as such, but in the criticisms of the measure
there has been shown some misunderstanding as to the intentions of the government at the time the legislation was first placed on the statute books of the dominion.
It will be recalled that from 1931 to 1937 there was a period of severe drought in western Canada, and during that period we paid out large sums of money from the federal treasury. It is in my memory that $186,000,000 was paid out of the treasury of Canada for the purpose of maintaining persons in what is known as the drought area of western Canada. Having made that enormous expenditure, or at least committed ourselves to credits which resulted in that expenditure finally, the government thought it was necessary for some action to be taken to assure the people of the district that certain assistance would be available under certain circumstances.
It will be recalled that during the period from 1931 to 1937 farmers had to go to councils and plead for relief. The result was that certain amounts were allowed per person in order to maintain the individual in food and clothing. It was thought by the government that if that condition were allowed to continue in an area that was populated by about a million people, in due course it would be depopulated. Any young person who finds himself or herself dressed in other people's clothes when he goes to school or to church will not remain in a district which compels that for a very long period of time; they will get out just as soon as they can. It was decided that an area which had contributed so much wealth to the Dominion of Canada should not be depopulated. The experience of having kept these people there has proven to us that the contention was the correct one. Everything that was done by previous dominion governments and by provincial governments and municipalities has proven to have been useful because, during the last six years, when this country was one of the allied countries at war that particular area produced more tonnage of food than it ever did in any other six years of its existence. In other words, the experience of having kept people on that land to produce has resulted in showing that we could not have contributed as we did during the war period to the feeding of the allied armies and Britain in the manner in which we did had that area not been opened, and it has proven, too, that an area which can produce that much wealth over any five, six or seven-year period should be kept in production during the other five, six or seven year periods during which crops are not sufficiently great to' maintain population there.
3S26

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
That was the idea behind the legislation, but there is a further fact which we should recall at this time. Prior to the enactment of this legislation, the legal and constitutional responsibility for taking care of people in those areas rested on the province and on the municipalities; it rested first on the provinces, and then by provincial law much of it was placed upon the municipalities individually. That is one of the reasons why the blocks are maintained. The federal government considered that in taking the solid blocks they were taking on the responsibility that should be placed on all the people of Canada.
Prior to the introduction of this act, we assumed the responsibility if twenty-five municipalities in a province found themselves unable to maintain their people, and when they got down to having only ten we ceased to assist. Under this act we have said, down to the present time, that if the government declared a year an emergency year, then the federal government assumed responsibility for the solid blocks of people to whom it was found necessary to give some assistance in order that they might be able to remain in that area. We have however, said over and over again from 1939 to the present, every time that we have received a resolution, such as that which was just placed on Hansard, from a municipality in the heart of the drought area, no matter what government was carrying on in the province, that the federal government is not taking the full responsibility; that part of the responsibility must rest on the province, and that if the province so decides, part of it must still rest on the municipality. Therefore we have said what the province ought to do, if they desire us to go farther than we have gone, is to make some contribution into the fund to take care of those corners in certain areas which are not included when the act says it must be a rectangle and when you say it must be contiguous to an area which is already proven to be a drought area. The dominion government believes that the areas which are immediately roundabout the solid block should be taken care of through the province and the municipality contributing something. If it is desired that the administration should be carried on under one set-up we are satisfied to conduct that administration; but if it were thought that it should be conducted under some other set-up, provincial or municipal, I am sure that we would cooperate in every way possible to see that that is carried out.

That is the reason why we placed in the act in the first place the provision that it Should be solid blocks and that these blocks should be on a township basis. Later, we took in a greater part of the area by consenting to take in areas of ten townships or more which were contiguous to the larger block, but we still think the others should accept some responsibility once the greater part of the area is dealt with.
There is one other reason why we have maintained the solid block or the township areas, and I may say that when the legislation was amended before it was the intention that [DOT] when a nine section area was added it should be treated under the terms of the different regulations and terms of the act as though it were an entire township.
There is another reason why we have taken the six-mile square block as the unit, and it is largely the reason which was brought out by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross). He said that in his opinion people who have had payments time after time-probably he would say townships which have had payments for so many continuous years-should be eliminated. We sought to meet the same contention when the act was first brought in by saying that the blocks had to be six miles square, and that instead of paying on an

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
individual basis we would pay on a township basis. The reason was that it will be found certain areas within those townships should not be farmed at all, and we have made provision under P.F.R.A. to organize those areas into community pastures, as was suggested by the bon. member for Souris. We have made provision also to stand the expense of moving farmers out of those areas into better areas; and, having done that, we think the federal government has done its share in trying to reestablish these people. Then we say to them, "If you insist on remaining in a township where two-thirds of the land is good and produces good crops every year and one-third of the land is poor and produces poor crops every year, it should not be considered the responsibility of the government to take care of you every year." In other words, instead of removing'areas in the manner suggested by the hon. member for Souris, and on such a wide scale, we have tried to provide against people coming under the terms of the act who insist upon remaining on what everyone recognizes to be submarginal land.
In the act we had another protection against the thing that was feared by the hon. member for Souris; and only today, when I read the bill over carefully after coming into the house, I found that the provision in question had been eliminated from the definition in the present legislation. I am not too sure that when we get into committee we should not consider putting back that protection. In the definition of "cultivated land" the last words were, "and which has not reverted to natural prairie." That provision was inserted in 1939 because, as hon. members know, there were at least a million and a half acres of land in western Canada, much of which had been cultivated over a long period of years, which during the seven years of drought had not been cultivated, or had been allowed to go back to prairie. Perhaps it was just blowing around the country, and was not even growing grass. We said, if that land was brought back under cultivation, payments would not be made on it under this act; and the provision under which it was possible for the administration to carry out that idea was contained in those words, "and which has not reverted to natural prairie." I know there have been some hardships in applying that portion of the regulations, but you cannot apply legislation of this kind over a large area without having some hardships.
I want to repeat that the unit of six square miles was inserted in the act in the first place to provide that people who insisted on remaining on submarginal lands within the area were not paid each year, and
also to see to it that those who lived in areas which were subject to drought year after year, but still had good crops, were not denied the privileges of the act.
I should like to deal for just a moment with one other matter bearing upon the same point. Those who discuss the measure without fully understanding it-I am not speaking of members of this house but those outside- usually speak in terms of yield of wheat. One reason we are removing the section which provided that a man with 3,000 bushels of wheat could not collect is because yield of wheat really has nothing at all to do with the payments. A man may draw if he never grows a bushel of wheat. A man may draw if he summer-fallows all his land in a year and does not seed anything. A man may draw if he has all his land in pasture and only runs cattle. The only reason wheat is in there is to provide a barometer; and that barometer simply says that if the yield of wheat over a whole township is eight bushels an acre or less, then it must have been dry. That is all it says, and that is all wheat is in for.	When the inspectors
go out and go over a township it is not even necessary for them to visit every farm to. find out whether it has been dry. They have been compelled to do so, and thus increase the costs of administering the act, by the criticism that has been made. If they do not call on the farmer, there is some criticism; and if they do not examine the crop carefully there is still further criticism.

subtopic: CROP FAILURE PAYMENTS-AWARDS TO FARMERS WITH MINIMUM PRODUCTION
speechtext: Was my impression wrong, then, that when this act was first brought in and the limit of 3,000 bushels was imposed, that was done because it was felt that a person who had 3,000 bushels did not require assistance to pull through the year and put in his next crop?

subtopic: CROP FAILURE PAYMENTS-AWARDS TO FARMERS WITH MINIMUM PRODUCTION
speechtext:
As I remember it, the
3.000	bushels provision was not there when the act was first brought in; it was amended later. I believe that was put there at a time when we were doing other things in connection with wheat. At the time I believe we were paying something over and above the market price of wheat; we were paying eighty cents when wheat was worth sixty-two cents. Under those circumstances, the matter was discussed, and the principle I am outlining now was not accepted by those who were considering the matter at that time. I believe I am wrong when I say this was done when wheat was sixty-two cents. That was in 1938, the year before the act came in, so it was later than that; it was when some special provision was being made which left out the 5,000 bushels
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

in connection with deliveries to elevators; I have just forgotten the circumstances in connection with it. It has been agreed that wheat does not govern the decision as to whether payment will be made to an individual. Wheat governs only the decision as to whether or not it was dry in that area. One can understand that one might go to a farm where a man was raising live stock almost entirely, where he had perhaps only fifty acres of summer-fallow in wheat. That would be the best cultivated land on the farm. All of it might have been in summer-fallow the }mar previous, so that he would grow only one crop in two years. He might have twenty bushels to the acre on those fifty acres, and the remainder of a section of land might be devoted to growing feed for live stock, and pasture. Those who argue for the individual basis would say that, because he had twenty bushels to the acre of wheat on fifty acres, he should not be paid. It was never intended that the provision in relation,to wheat should be applied in that way at all. Wheat has nothing to do with it, other than it was felt we could determine whether or not it had been dry over a whole township by determining whether or not the wheat yield was eight bushels to the acre or less. But if it was twenty bushels to the acre over the whole township we are pretty well assured that it was not dry. Once the decision has been reached that it was dry, we go ahead and pay everyone in the municipality, in order to take care of the people who are raising live stock as well as grain.

subtopic: CROP FAILURE PAYMENTS-AWARDS TO FARMERS WITH MINIMUM PRODUCTION
speechtext: You mean in the township?

subtopic: CROP FAILURE PAYMENTS-AWARDS TO FARMERS WITH MINIMUM PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Yes, in the township. We pay everyone; and if all the townships in the municipality are in, we pay everyone in the municipality. We do that whether they are raising wheat, oats or barley; whether their farm is all in pasture, provided that they are not ranchers and have not irrigation; and we also pay when they have very small areas in wheat and the greater part of the farm taken up in the production of live stock. We think that is fair. The only unfair thing about it is this. If a man produces nothing but live stock; if he sells no grain, he does not pay in at all because all that he pays in is one per cent of the grain he sells. If he does not sell any grain at all. but sells all live stock, then he has an advantage over the man who grows nothing but grain. But, as hon. members- know, there are not so many of those men in the area we are talking about. Practically all of them have more acreage in grain than they utilize in producing live stock. 
But the reason for making it a unit is to determine whether it was dry or not, or simply finding out what the average yield over the whole township was. One could not find that out by taking the average yield of any one man's farm, because in some cases the man's yield would be twenty bushels, for the reasons I have spoken of, and in others it would be very low because he is farming land that he should not be farming at all. So we have tried to eliminate those possibilities by this provision. [DOT]
I think that is all I desire to say at the moment. It is my intention, immediately the bill gets second reading, to move that it be sent to the committee on agriculture and colonization. I hope that in that committee we can discuss all the details which have been raised in the discussion here by those who do not belong to the committee, and that when the bill comes back to be considered in committee of the whole we can go farther into any of the details which were raised and which may require to be discussed at greater length. I only wanted to say what I have said in order to recall again to the minds of hon. members the principles underlying the establishment of the legislation in the first place, and the manner in which we have attempted to carry it out.

subtopic: CROP FAILURE PAYMENTS-AWARDS TO FARMERS WITH MINIMUM PRODUCTION
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister one question before second reading is given. The interpretation is not quite clear now to some of us. When the act is amended as is proposed, will it mean that it will include any type of crop failure, through hail and everything else?

speechtext: It has always included any type of crop failure which was within an area where the crop was below eight bushels to the acre. But if the hail is in an area- and criticism on this score was, I think, raised by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. McKay)-where the average crop in the district is twenty bushels to the acre, but the hail runs right through the middle and takes a strip one or two miles wide, such people are not eligible for payment unless they are tributary to an area which is already in. The reason why that provision was made in that way was that two of the provinces have hail insurance legislation; and I am not sure but that there are three. Three did at one time have hail insurance legislation. Is Manitoba still in the hail insurance, or have they dropped it?

speechtext: No.

speechtext:
They have dropped it.

speechtext:
I think they have
dropped it. But the other provinces where the greater part of the drought area is have had hail insurance legislation. They can have it because they are provinces. The dominion parliament has not the authority to bring in insurance legislation. That question was determined in the years when we were discussing hail insurance. It was finally determined that the provincial government had the authority to do that, and the provincial government did bring it in. In Saskatchewan today, a farmer has the right over all the area where hail prevails-and he has not the right in the other because he has not desired to come into it-to collect under the hail insurance law which exists in the provinces. If he, of his own volition, decides to come out from under that, which he has the right to do under the legislation, there is no reason why any other piece of legislation should take care of him. He has legislation now which takes care of him. and he must sign himself out or it will take care of him. If he himself does not sign out personally, the whole municipality has to sign in or sign out in order to make the legislation operative or inoperative. When they have that right now I do not think, in this legislation, we should be asked to provide for it a second time. The provision is there now in the provincial law.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, June 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent for the second reading of Bill No. 253, to make provision with respect to forces of the United States of America when visiting Canada and with respect to the exercise of discipline and to the internal administration of such forces, and of the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Probe.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
When the house
adjourned last night I was pointing out that the United States had its own individual policy in world affairs and that by allying ourselves, as we are, with them so closely, we shall be drawn into their quarrels willy-nilly. It is also pertinent to point out at this time that the United States has a terrific economic stake in this country, and that the bringing in of the military in this way is just adding the final touch. In the final analysis it will at
least solve one question, namely the flag issue. All the Americans will have to do will be to stick nine more stars on their flag and that will finish it. Either that, or we can create one with a bald-headed eagle carrying a wet muskrat in its claws, and that would be our national flag; because we shall then have military as well as economic dictatorship in this country, and the government will be nothing more than trustees for United States capital.
As regards the attitude of United States personnel when they come into this country, granting them their own courts does not instil into them respect for our laws and customs. Many of the people of the United States are of' the highest type, but they also have their trouble in that country. In Prince Rupert, during the war, for instance, two aldermen who were walking down the street minding their own business were slugged down in the dark by United States soldiers. Owing to the persistence of one of the aldermen, the assailants were tracked down and tried by their own military courts. We never did know whether justice was meted out or not. I am afraid that sort of thing would come back once again. Their customs are different from ours. They have not the same respect for law and order. If they are allowed to come in here in a unit, with their own courts, they will certainly look on us as just another one of the conquered countries. I am absolutely opposed to it at the present time, because I believe it will give the yellow press of the United States some more ammunition in its witch-hunt on communism. If you read history you will find that any time any movement is persecuted bitterly, it grows and thrives on persecution. History has always taught us that. The only way in which we can bring in a higher order of society if we wish to do so, is conr sciously to adapt ourselves to changing times and instil in the people faitn in their own democracy. This witch-hunt will certainly create the very opposite to what it is supposed to do. It is a sign of fear on the part of the people who are conducting it. They are afraid. They have no faith in their own institutions or in their own intellect. Let us have people who have faith in their institutions; then that faith will be instilled in the people, and there will be no more of this ranting and raving about some foreign ideology. We talk about the Russians going into such countries as Poland, Roumanda, Hungary, and so on. We are doing it here by act of parliament, giving the works away. Let us turn this down and throw it out of court, because it will only breed fear and suspicion.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations on the bill. I had not the good fortune to hear the interesting debate last night; but it seems to me that it made perfectly clear that this bill takes us far afield into matters of tremendous international importance in which we, whether we like it or not, are deeply and inescapably involved.
I should like to say, in passing, that I have no fear whatever of any ulterior motive on the part of the United States being involved in this bill. I am perfectly prepared to accept the statement of military authorities that this bill is, in many ways, a natural process. But it has become clear, I think, during the course of the debate, that certain important questions are involved, which have been adequately discussed and which I do not intend to take the time of the house in discussing at the present time.
What I wish to speak about for a few minutes is that all-important question which lies at the root of this whole matter and which has been referred to more than once in this debate; namely the relations between the United States and the U.S.S.R. I suppose if there is anything upon which we can all agree, it is that we are deeply grieved1 at the tremendous deterioration in international relations in the last eighteen months. For that we blame the Russians, and, for all I can see, we are entitled to blame them.
It does seem to me that there was in San Francisco about two years ago-perhaps a little more than two years ago-a readiness for cooperation which could have brought the results for which we thought we were fighting. It is now made clear that in the weary months which have followed there has been very little cooperation from the U.SB.R. And, such as there has been, looking at it as fairly as we can, seems to have come only under pressure, only when we have been, as it is called, tough.
Therefore we have come to the conclusion- and I do not see how we can come to any other conclusion-that we have to be firm. The premier of Ontario, who has just returned from Europe, tells us that today and I do not see how we can disagree with him. We have to be firm. We say that we must not have appeasement, because that gets us nowhere; and I do not disagree with that.
But I should like to say-and perhaps this is the real comment I wish to make this afternoon-that firmness is not enough. Firmness, in itself, is not a policy. Therefore I wish to suggest that there are one or two other things we should have in our minds beyond firmness.
I want to suggest that, as in nearly all human [Mr. Archibald.)
relations, the fault is not all on one side; and when we are considering a thing like this, which I think in moderate language we can say is in very truth, a matter of life and death to us, and to our children-it seems to me that we should be very honest with ourselves, as well as very honest with those with whom we disagree. I think we should try to believe that in the end good sense will prevail; because, if it does not, then surely we can say again, using what I hope are not exaggerated words, that there is very little reason to believe that our civilization will persist.
We have talked in the past about the tremendous things which would result from the discovery of new weapons. It seems to me that now we have discovered new weapons which seem different, not only in degree but also in kind, from those which we have been used to before. Therefore I should like to remind the house-and I think we should remind ourselves-that, although I do not doubt that the Russian government is very well informed as to the true state of feeling in this country, nevertheless statements are being made from time to time in the United States and no doubt, if they are relayed to the Russian people, they can be used by the Russian government to suggest to the Russian people that there are imperialistic designs on the part of the United States against them.
I do not believe that to be so for a moment. But I do believe that things are said which can readily be made to bear that interpretation. And in that connection I should like to read a brief statement from that moderate and sensible publication, the London Spectator, which says:
The increasingly impatient and unfriendly attitude of -the American majority to the Soviet Union is a real danger.
Personally I do not believe there is an unfriendly attitude on the part of the American majority; and I shall have a word to say about that later. But I have quoted this as the opinion of a responsible journal because it could be used to show that the Russian government, in trying to alarm its people, has some basis of justification.
What is the truth of the situation? Do any of us believe that there is one one-hundredth of one per cent of the 130,000,000 people of the United States who do not abhor the very thought of war. And does not one believe that that is true with regard to an equally vast number in Russia?
I read the other day an interesting report by an American who had just returned from Europe, and who had been travelling widely on that continent. He said that he never found

Visiting Forces
anywhere that people were interested in war or were talking about war. What they were interested in was housing, food, and clothing, the reestablishment of their families and bringing themselves back to some kind of a civilized life again. Then he added that it was not until he got back to the United States and stepped out of his plane that he began to hear people talking about war. I am not suggesting that many people are talking about war, but I am suggesting that there have been careless statements in the United States, some of which have come from high military authorities, which may have been sufficient, as I say, to enable the Russian government to mislead their people, and to make them believe that there are motives of unfriendliness in the United States against them.
I suppose it is true to say that in the past a good many wars have been fought, to some extent at any rate, from economic motives. But can anyone suggest that either of these two great continental powers need to fight a war or go to war for economic motives? I do not think any person would suggest that. If it is done it will be from fear and from ideological motives. So I say that we have a situation which makes the thought of war in one -way absolutely fantastic; yet, on the other hand, I know people will say, "Well, what is the use of talking about it? The Russian people have no say about what happens. They are in a police state and just like a lot of pawns."
I remember a play some years ago which had as its subject a principality in India. The prince was an absolute monarch. He was asked why he did not do such and such a thing. His reply was-and I thought it interesting at the time, because it is profoundly true even in a police state-"Even the most absolute monarch can only act with the consent of the governed." In a way, probably that is a paradox; and yet I wonder after all if it is so paradoxical. We believe that Hitler had convinced his people so that they were ready to go along with him. I suppose, in a way, that the Russian government have convinced their people, too. And, of course, they were attacked.
Now a word or two as to what I think this adds up to. I do not suggest that we should disregard defence. I do not suggest that we should give up the military advantages we have at the present time. I think we are forced to say, and that we may properly say to the Russians: "You are maintaining your huge army, greater than that of any other army in the world. True, we in America have the atomic bomb, but we have to have a counterpoise to your army."
But I do say this, that at the present time we have a situation which reminds me of a condition which we will all remember when we were boys, when two small boys would shoulder up against each other, with the final result that one would haul off and paste the other-and the fight was on. We have something very much like that now. I suggest, first of all, that it is part of the responsibility of people everywhere-of course, what we can say or do here will matter little; one can carry only one's own load and speak one's own view for what it is worth-that we should refuse to tolerate the idea that war is coming and accept it as a kind of inevitability. I sometimes think we have begun to forget what it is like. A great many in this house have been through the war; some of them have been through two wars, and I think we are all apt to feel, "Oh, well, those prophecies were made and they did not come true." They came true enough in Europe; they came true enough if we are to believe what we have heard from those who have been there.
The next thing I would say is that we should have a strong sense of responsibility in what we say. I ran across two things which had been said'by Mr. Walter Lippmann, who, I think, is one of the wise men of today. I should like to quote them because I believe they are true. This is what he said about the Russians and the atom bomb:
They know we shall not use it against them unless they do what they do not intend to do [DOT] precipitate a general war.
Here is a further quotation about Russia:
They are in no danger and they know they are in no danger of being attacked by the United States.
We all believe that is true and, of course, if the Russian people believed it was true I think there would be no danger of war. It may be said that there are no means of getting that through to them, but I think that is only a half truth. We have had a great deal of evidence to show that the Russian soldiers who were in Europe saw even in shattered Europe a way of life far above their own. They compared it with their own way of life, and we have a great deal of evidence to show that they took back the impressions of what they had seen. We can be sure that the Russian government knows the truth.
The last thing I want to say is this: People will say, "Well, there is not much hope in that; what you are suggesting is that we should be moderate, that we should try to see the other side, that we should curb ourselves from saying things which can be used by this
Visiting Forces

unscrupulous Russian government to poison the minds of their people." I do not know whether there is much hope in that, but all I want to say is that if there is not much hope in that, if it is not worth our while to work to that end, hoping that in the end, in some way which perhaps we cannot now see, better counsels will prevail, then I say there is not much hope in anything.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words to say in support of the bill now under discussion. I am in agreement with those who advocate that we should not give up part of our sovereignty; but in view of the fact that certain circumstances now exist in the world, in view of the fact that we have practically the same economic interests as the United States, our friendly neighbour, I do not see why we should make so much fuss over this bill and be so afraid of giving up too much of our sovereignty to the United States. I heard the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) say last night that we should not play Russia's game. I agree absolutely with him. Then I heard other hon. members say that the same privileges should be extended to every nation of the world. Perhaps 1 should be excused, but I really cannot make any sense out of such a proposition.
The hon. member for Vancouver North stated that it would be foolish to ask this government and this parliament to extend to the U.S.S.R., Yugoslavia and Hungary the same privileges being extended to the United States, a great, powerful and friendly nation. We cannot compare the friendship of Russia toward Canada with the friendship of the United States toward our country. It is impossible; we cannot do it. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), "'ho has just taken his seat, said that we must look at both sides. It is easy now to look at both sides.
If you read the article in Newsweek of last week you must realize that you cannot overlook the dangerous infiltration of communism into the United States and Canada, an infiltration which is spreading its tentacles even into churches. We are not ready to extend these special privileges to the armi of the U.S.S.R. when tomorrow we might be faced with an economic revolution w'hich was developed and encouraged by this infiltration of what my hon. friend has just called the witch of communism. I am afraid of that kind of witch and I am ready to fight it anywhere and everywhere.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: He is fighting too.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
He does not look like it. If we wake up tomorrow and are faced with that kind of revolution it will be too bad for those who have been so short-sighted. My last reason for being in favour of the bill is that the Russians are against it. I have before me the Montreal Gazette of June 2. Once in a while we find something interesting in the Montreal Gazette. This article reads:
London, June 2-(Reuters)-Moscow radio said in a news broadcast today that Canadians were getting "more and more uneasy" about impending "infiltration" of L'nited States troops, consequent upon plans for United States-Cana-dian defence cooperation.
A nd again:
"In this draft," the broadcast said, "United States troops are given such privileges that have never before been given to foreign troops on territories of other countries in peace time."
Indirectly Russia is asking for the same privileges, and that idea is echoed in this house. The article continues:
"Several articles of the Canadian criminal code will not be applied to the U.S. troops. Military and other U.S. authorities are granted full rights on the Canadian territory, providing only that they do not interfere with the local Canadian ones."
"Several observers consider that the final approval of this draft will be only a further step toward Canada's final subservience to the U.S.A."
I am not afraid of any subservience we may show to the United States. If the United States had wanted to get Canada before, they had many opportunities to do so, and everyone knows it. I think we should rather cultivate the friendship of the United States than try to keep what is left of the friendship of Generalissimo Stalin, who has just called us a weak nation. Maybe my hon. friends who propose to give the same privileges to Russian troops as it is proposed to extend to United States troops will bow down before Mr. Stalin, calling us a weak nation. But in mjr opinion, Canada, with its great natural resources and its strong and virile population, must show Mr. Stalin that we are strong and clear-sighted enough to see what might come upon us through the infiltration of his spies even in this very country. We must not be content with a false sense of security. In view of what has happened lately in this country, we must be more far-sighted and not wait until the revolution comes upon us to give the United States the largest measure of friendship that we can give them. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, for the close friendship that we must extend to the United States and for the safety of my country, I gladly support this bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the speech of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) last evening constituted a strong argument for the terms of the amendment now before the house to the effect that Bill No. 253 should not now be read a second time but rather that its subject matter be referred to the standing committee on external affairs.
The Minister of National Defence gave us certain information regarding what he referred to as a similar act in the United States, and in giving us details of that act he pointed out that it is quite different from the measure now before the house. The act in the United States referred to is the Friendly Foreign Forces Act, andl so far as the act itself is concerned it is general in its application rather than having specific reference to one country as does the bill now before this house. The minister went on to point out that only such countries came under the provisions of the United States Act as are covered by a presidential proclamation, and he gave the terms of one such presidential proclamation which brought the United Kingdom and Canada within the provisions of that act. I noticed, however, that the reference to the United Kingdom and Canada in that presidential proclamation was to these two countries as co-belligerents with the United States. I am not going to go into any further details with regard to the Friendly Foreign Forces Act, but it does seem to me that the information which the, minister has given to the house is sufficient to indicate that we should examine carefully whether the bill before us is the kind of bill that we should be passing at all. I, for one, think that if we are to have a bill of this nature it should be similar to the United States act in that it should be general in its application. But even with regard to the United States act I should like to be able to ask questions as to the significance of that word "co-belligerents". Surely we are not at war at the present time, and therefore I am opposed' to this kind of legislation. In these circumstances it is not good enough to ask the house to give second reading to this bill on the usual understanding that we can make amendments when we are in committee of the whole, because we know we do not get very far along that track. It seems to me desirable that the whole subject before us be referred to the committee on external, affairs where members can discuss the issues involved with the minister, and I am sure that the minister, from the experience we have already had on that committee, will be only too glad1 to accept
the advice and considered opinion of the committee. I hope, therefore, that it will not be necessary for us to vote on this amendment, but that, the government will realize that, it is a good suggestion and will agree to permit the subject matter of this bill to go to that committee.
