subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
I have all the objections to it that have been stated1 by other hon. members, including in particular the, remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) last evening, and the pointed remarks just now made by the hon member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell).
The main fact of the present world situation, on which this bill has a bearing, is, as was stated last night by the hon. member for Vancouver South, the tragic way in which the world is tending to divide itself into two camps. I can appreciate the sentiments of the hon. member (Mr. Gauthier) who has just taken bis seat when he'referred to the desirability of building up a strong friendly relationship with our great neighbour, the United States of America.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
And of
maintaining it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
And of maintaining that relationship for all time. But I wish to point out to the hon. member and to this house that the possibility, not merely of maintaining that friendship, but of actually keeping in existence two countries like the United States and Canada depends upon our world being kept going at all. In other words, our destiny as a nation and the destiny of North America depends upon the maintenance of the peace of the world. We can no longer think in terms of adequate defence for a nation or a continent or a hemisphere. We have to see to it that war itself does not break out again.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario was very much to the point when he talked of how people generally are saying that the dire prophecies about the last war did not come true and maybe we can survive another world war. He was quite right when he said that for great sections of the world the dire prophecies had come true in the tragic destruction visited on large sections of the earth, and furthermore, in the terrific economic and social mal-
Visiting Forces

adjustments we are facing the world over today. I maintain that if we are sensible human beings we simply cannot think at all of pursuing any course that would lead to another war. If you accept the possibility of there being another war and the possibility of civilization surviving another war, why, then, there is logic to this discussion of ways arid means of defending ourselves on a national, continental, or hemisphere basis. But if you face the fact that we simply cannot have another war, that it means the end of everything, then we have to find new ways and means of avoiding it. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that dividing the world into two camps, dividing the world into power blocs, has been tried often enough and it has failed in the past and will fail again.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: It is easy enough to say that on your side.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: My hon. friend has made the statement that it is easy to make the statement that our side is in the right.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: It is, too.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: We always do that even in arguments which take place in the house; as for example, the exchanges between the Minister of Veterans Affairs and me. We have them often. I always think he is wrong; he always thinks I am wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
But I am right.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Many more think so than otherwise.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
I want to assure the house that that little dialogue was unrehearsed; but it does drive home my point. It reminds me of an experience I had a little over a year ago, in the month of February, 1946. It was then two or three days after the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had announced the investigation that was to take place into the espionage situation. By the strangest of coincidents I had the privilege at the time of being in Moscow, and on this occasion-it is particularly in my mind because of the little interchange that my right hon. friend and I have just had-there was a reception held at the Canadian embassy in Moscow. There were three Russian visitors; they were on a semiofficial level. One of them was a lady who was the head of the society for cultural relations with foreigners; the second was an army officer who maintained liaison relationships with military attaches of other embassies in Moscow, and the third person was an official from the protocol division of the Russian foreign office. As was natural,

because of the situation which had developed owing to the announcement about the espionage matter, we had quite a lengthy conversation. I will not go into all the details of that conversation, but it reached a point something like this. These people said to me: "What worries us is that the news which has come out"-they were not discussing the merits or demerits of the case at the moment -"has released such a flood of anti-soviet feeling and anti-soviet propaganda in the Canadian newspapers." That was the principal feature which was being reported in the Moscow newspapers at the time. I tried to explain the freedom of the press as we have it in this country, but we got along to the point where I tried to show to my three Russian friends to whom I was talking the real basic difficulty; I said, "I must admit that our western people are afraid of you, afraid there is going to be another war." With a response that was so ready that I could not avoid feeling it was genuine, they said to me: "Why are you afraid of us? We are the ones who are afraid of you." I was equally taken aback at the thought that they were afraid of us as being the people who might bring on another war. Our conversation carried on. There were five or six of us at this time because one or two of the Canadians had joined us, and we agreed that we had there the epitome of the world situation, a camp on one side afraid of the other, but not for one moment thinking that the reverse is the feeling over in the other camp.
Somehow or another we have to try to break that down. In my view we shall not break it down by adopting the attitude which my hon. friend suggests, always assuming that the other side is wrong. I do not mean to suggest that we go to the other extreme and always assume that we are wrong. What we have to do is to face the thing objectively and set as our aim the breaking down of this division into two camps and get the world together in some sort of international organization which, as the hon. member for Mus-koka-Ontario has just said, if there is not some hope in it, then there is no hope in anything.
During the course of this debate it has been said that we must be practical. I agree. The suggestion was made last night by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Baker) that those who talked in any other terms than regional defence arrangements such as this envisages are being unrealistic and that he was tired of that kind of thing. All of us, of course, can use that language. Wre all like to think that we

Visiting Forces
are the ones who are realistic and that it is the other fellow who is being impractical. I want to suggest that the most unrealistic approach in the world today is the approach that thinks we can defend ourselves by some sort of regional defence; that we can defend ourselves by tying up no longer with the British navy but by tying up to the might and power of the friendly nation to the south of us. That, Mr. Speaker, is completely unrealistic. The practical position today is to realize that there is no defence except to end war itself; that the destiny of this country, the destiny of Britain, the destiny of the United States, the destiny of all countries of the world is wrapped up in the maintenance of world peace for all time. It is that or nothing. We must make as our main aim, our main course, the following of ways and means that will somehow reverse the tragic trend which things have taken in the past few months.
I felt that the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario was describing the situation correctly when he referred to the deterioration that has taken place in relations between the western camp and the soviet camp in the last number of months. We must remember -and I hope that some day we can recapture it-the high idealism and the high hopes that were raised at the time of the San Francisco conference two years ago. At that time, although the war in Europe was over, V-J day had not yet come; and it was a mark of deep significance that here was a world which was not yet over a terrible war but which was already making plans to build an international organization that would keep the peace which was yet to be won.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Does the hon. member think we shall establish world peace by disarming and by not taking all the advantage we can of our allies, while Russia arms and is going through a systematic process of building up her armies? Does the hon. member think we can maintain peace by disarmament and breaking away from our allies; or by arming and showing that we can defend ourselves? I should like him to answer that. I am being practical now, but the hon. member has attacked me.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
I did not attack my hon. friend; I took his words and used them. The question that the hon. member has asked points up the very, thing that T am trying to say, namely, that in my view the
building of defences is based upon the premise that we are to have another war and that it is perfectly proper for the other fellow to build his defences too. That means that in due course we have a conflict and our defences on both sides are of no use whatsoever.
I believe the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario was not talking in paradoxical terms but was being pretty practical when he said we have to show firmness, we have to make it clear that we are not weak; yet at the same time, or, as he put it, we have to go farther and find ways and means of bridging the gap between these two camps and bringing them closer together.
Now I want now to come a little more closely to grips, if I can, with the point raised by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare, who referred to the way in which the Soviet Union is enlarging the number of states coming under its control. It is interesting to note the way in which we refer to the nations that come under the control of the Soviet Union as satellites of that power, and the way in which we refer to the troops of the Soviet Union in those other countries as being an outrage. And I quite agree; I do not deny it for a moment. But it is strange that when we have foreign troops on our own soil we call it a natural process, or working along with people of like-minded notions, or friendly relations with a friendly power. We are honest when we say these things; when hon. members use these phrases in this house during this debate that is what they mean, but it does not look that way to the people in the other camp, just as the things they are doing over on the other side of the world do not look like a natural process, or the soviets working along with people of like-minded notions, or friendly relations between friendly powers.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Who started it?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: My hon. friend means, who started this deterioration of relations between the Soviet Lbtion and the United States?

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: No; who started moving their troops into other countries?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
As far as the future is concerned, as far as maintaining world peace is concerned, it does not matter. When we have had an atomic war and we are all dead, it will not make much difference who started . the thing. What matters is that we put some thought and effort now into trying to prevent it.
I should like to get along now to what I consider a practical suggestion to try to put a stop to this policy which the United States,
Visiting Forces

on the one hand, and the Soviet Union, on the other, are pursuing. I think they are both wrong; and hon. members may take their choice as to who started it or who is the worst protagonist of the policy. I believe they are both wrong. I believe the Soviet Union should be condemned in strong language for what it has been doing by way of gathering in a larger number of satellites and trying to push out its frontiers, giving the western camp the feeling that war is coming. I think it is equally wrong for the United States to have gone beyond the famous Monroe doctrine to a Truman doctrine that extends the military and political barriers of the United States half way around the world. We are now being drawn into this United States policy; we are capitulating to it, and I think this country at this moment has a supreme opportunity. We can turn down this idea. We can say we are not going to have United States troops in Canada in peace time. That would be the first move by any small country against the Truman policy or the Stalin policy, and it would put us in the position of being able properly to criticize the Soviet Union for what they are doing as well as the United States. It would also strengthen our position in the councils of the united nations.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: It would make us absolutely helpless.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Not a bit of it. It would restore us to a moral position we are fast losing in the councils of the united nations. It took a long time for this country to convince the other nations of the world1 that we had an independent voice. We took a long step in that direction after the last war, when Canada was accepted as a signatory to the treaty of Versailles and as a member of the league of nations. It has taken a long while to convince the rest of the world that we are not just a daughter of the mother country, and that we speak for ourselves as an independent nation. Now, barely out of that era, we find ourselves being thought of by other nations of the world as a tool in United States foreign, economic and military policy.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
It is not nonsense at all. I had the privilege of attending one session of the united nations; and, while there, it was my experience that we were losing ground, not because of our close connection with the United Kingdom, but because of our close connection with the United States. I suggest and I insist that at future meetings of the united nations any attempt by Canada to express

views on this division of the world into two camps will simply not carry any weight at all, because we are part of the United States scheme; any more than to us the voice of Poland, or Yugoslavia carries any weight, because we say they are just expressing what is in the interests of the Soviet Union.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question? He mentioned that he attended one meeting, the first part of the first assembly of the united nations, and he spoke of the reputation Canada had at that meeting. To confine my question to that meeting, does the hon. gentleman know of any country whose reputation was any higher in its desire to collaborate in important matters affecting the peace of the world than Canada?

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: If he remained awake during the sitting he deserves a lot of credit.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Of course the question
is worded in such a way that you just cannot answer it; that is why the minister worded it as he did; but I will say to him that he knows we stood high on the first ballot for election to the security council. We did not get elected to that council, however, and it is my view that was largely because we were favoured by the United States, and-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: Surely that was not it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: I got around and talked to a good many people, too. I did not waste any time while I was there.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Perhaps
they looked at some of our representatives.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
I beg your pardon?
These interruptions mean just one thing. They mean something is being said that is hitting home. I know just as surely as that I am standing here that at the next meeting of the united nations, with United States troops on Canadian soil and the whole infiltration that is going on into our national life, our voice on these matters, as I have said already, will not carry any more weight with those on the other side than does the voice of Yugoslavia or Poland with us when they speak on these same matters.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Your voice won't be
there.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: The voice of Canada will be there.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Then how do you explain that Canada was elected for the longest term possible to the economic and social council, at the same time as it was up for election to the security council?

Visiting Forces

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
It is because that council
is not of any importance at all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Oh, no. I may argue
with my hon. friend the Minister of National Health and Welfare. (Mr. Martin), but I cannot agree with the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) on that. To me the most hopeful feature of the united nations is the economic and social council; and one of the things I am really proud of is that Canada played such an important part at San Francisco in helping to get the provision for the economic and social council written into the charter. I think that was one of the reasons Canada was accorded such a high position on that council at London.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to conclude, I want to put before the house and before the government as a serious suggestion the thought that the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has posed the problem very well, and that we must try to find some way to reverse the deterioration which is now taking place in relations between the western camp and the soviet camp. We will not reverse the trend by allowing ourselves to be pulled into the western camp. WTe might have a chance to reverse it if we stopped this trend and, by prohibiting United States troops coming onto our soil, put ourselves in the strong moral position of being able to speak with an independent voice and to play, not a lesser but' a greater part than we have played in the past in the councils of the united nations, which, despite what has been said by the hon. member for Temiscouata, to me holds out the only hope for peace in the future. Let us not, on the one hand, boast of our membership in the united nations and talk of the great principles of collective security, and, on the other, follow the old methods of regional defence, the old ideas which led to war; for in our day war is no longer something which we can have and survive. War is something that means the end of everything. In the name of the people of this country whom we represent, in the name of humanity-the welfare of which is the purpose of the united nations-let us use some real sense and try to grapple with this problem in an effective and practical way.
I close with this final plea to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), that he see the meaning and the value in the suggestion which we have made that this whole matter go to the external affairs committee before second reading, and that he therefore accept the amendment made by my colleague the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe).

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
I am very much interested in what the previous speakers have said, and in the changes in the policies of hon. gentlemen to my left. I remember the position which those hon. gentlemen took in this house during the dark days six months before the war broke out in 1939. They said, "Let us depend on Washington for peace. What have we to do with Britain's wars?" One of them wanted to reduce the defence estimates of my hon. friend the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), who was then Minister of National Defence. I called the attention of the house to the six hundred miles of unprotected coastline in British Columbia, from Puget sound to the southern Queen Charlotte islands, which had no defence at all if the British fleet were withdrawn from the Pacific in the event of war which I saw coming. After the war started, I said to these gentlemen, "Where are now you prophets who prophesied?"-as the hon. gentleman and the minister are prophesying tonight. I quoted Jeremiah, chapter 37, verse 19, to those gentlemen:
Where are now your prophets which prophesied unto you, saying, The King of Babylon shall not come against you, nor against this land?
These hon. gentlemen, six months before the war broke out, believed in the policy that our defencelessness was our greatest asset. In March, 1939, I moved the adjournment of the house to discuss the matter and told them that war was just about on us, and all that kind of thing. Now what do they say? What does the leader of the party say? Miss Agnes MacPhail, who is not now a member of the house but who at that time represented the constituency of Grey-Bruce, said, "Why do we need to go looking for defence across the water to Glasgow and to London", that we could get all the defence we wanted at Washington and to remember we were on the North American continent. That was the policy of the pacifists. They believed in peace pacts, peace notes, the league of nations, agreements and all that kind of thing-something which caused this second war as well as the first one. I would go as far as anybody in this house in paying respect and showing admiration for the cooperation of the people of the United States. But do not forget this. Had we depended on hon. gentlemen to my left and on Washington for defence, and not on the British fleet, what would have happened? That fleet gave us and all America protection for 200 years. It was the British fleet that saved American shores before the war started. That fleet was the real Monroe doctrine.
Visiting Forces

Where would we have been if we had adopted the policy of hon. gentlemen in the C.C.F.? We would have been invaded, and we were very close to being in that position. The hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot) made a fine speech last night. In some respects I agree with what he said. The axis fleet was right up along the coast of Newfoundland, in the St. Lawrence and other places like that. We were very close to being invaded.
The hon. gentleman who preceded me did not refer to the bill at all, or its object or principles.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext: I dealt with the amendment, and that is what is before the house.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
He was one of those to whom I referred when I quoted Jeremiah, who put his dependence in peace pacts, our defencelessness and all the rest of it. But Winnipeg, in which his constituency is situated, raised a large force of magnificent troops when Canada was at war.
I wish now to come to Bill No. 253 and bring the house back to what we are discussing. The bill is based on the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on February 12 last, which deals with seven clauses and different aspects of defence and collaboration with the great nation to the south of us to whom we owe so much.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the recess at six o'clock I had been referring to our hon. friends to my left, and had stated that they were not the only pacifists in 1939 in the country. The debate then on the reduction in the estimates speaks for itself.
I wish to deal with the principle of the bill, because that is what is before us on second reading. True it is that the speeches come within the wide latitude given by the Prime Minister when he addressed the house on February 12 of this year, upon which occasion he outlined six or seven means of collaboration with the United States in respect of defence. No doubt what the Prime Minister said on that occasion has influenced some members who have spoken in this debate.
What is this bill? It is to make provision for the discipline and internal administration of visiting forces of the United States of America, when present in Canada with the consent of the government of Canada. The

provisions of the criminal code, which are declared inapplicable to members of the United States forces, are applicable to the other dominions. They apply to Australia, New Zealand and to the other dominions within the empire, but not to the United States.
The sections in the criminal code I refer to have reference to unlawful drilling, the use of offensive weapons and many other matters. I would call the attention of the house to the principle of the bill, because as we look at the world today we look at a very dark picture indeed. Two years ago, at the close of the war, Great Britain and her dominions stood at the pinnacle of their strength, and stood as a bulwark for the protection of civilization, liberty, and all that kind of thing. During four centuries Britain has saved the world and the empire from a slavery worse than death. I refer to the days of Philip of Spain, Louis XIV, Napoleon, and even twice in our own generation against the axis powers.
The New York Times, in a recent article dealing with this matter said:
From the day_ it broke away from the British empire -the United States has been living in large measure under the protection of that empire and in particular, of the British fleet.
This was not necessarily an altruistic action on the -part of Britain, but in days when Europe was the world's powerhouse and when Britain held the predatory European empires, it was to her own best interests to keep other European powers out of the western hemisphere. It was this interest which inspired the Monroe doctrine which was proclaimed by the United States.as its own, and was really made effective by the British fleet.
It was the same interest which in the final analysis safeguarded the freedom of all the Americas.
That is absolutely correct; it is the verdict of history. When I speak with respect to the principle of the bill, I would also, as have other members, speak about the duty this country owes to the people of the United States. In that connection I would point out that in my view the bill before the house violates the principles of the Rush-Bagot treaty. It is an absolute violation of that treat}'. There is no doubt that we owe a great deal to the United States, and it is possible that our collaboration with them and Britain may save us from a third war, or, as F. D. Roosevelt called it, a war of survival. There can be no doubt about that. If we are to save the world, then the western democracies, Great Britain and the United States, must have absolute cooperation and collaboration in all important matters, and protest now against Russian plans to dominate the world.

Visiting Forces
I believe that throughout the war we surrendered too much initiative to Washington in our military, political, economic, social and financial spheres. I am one who believes we have gone too far in that direction, and the United States would have more respect for us if we told them that. I still maintain that patriotism is the cement which binds nations together.
In the Lay of the Last Minstrel, Sir Walter Scott said:
Breathes there the man, with soul so dead, Who never to himself hath said,
This is my own, my native land!
And, doubly dying shall go down
To the vile dust, from whence he sprung,
Unwept, unlionour'd, and unsung.
I believe there are some people in this country who do not appreciate those lines. In the first and second great wars we were saved from war on our own soil by Britain's magnificent fleet, when the enemy came right to our gates. Portions of the axis fleet were right in the gulf of the St. Lawrence, around Newfoundland, and we were saved by the British fleet from the awful results of invasion of our own soil.
Let me repeat that in my view this bill is in violation of the principles of the Rush-Bagot- treaty. I do not know who has asked for the measure. I am wondering what the effect will be when it is read alongside the statement made by that great President Truman who will visit this country within a few days. I know he will be received with open arms, as a tribute to a great nation of which it is his honour to be the President. But it was only on Monday last he issued a statement in which he advised the United States to arm, or to invite extermination. A commission to look into military training has been operating in the United States, and its statement speaks for itself. The President asks for $1,750 million each year for universal training of those from eighteen years of age up.
In view of the statement made last Monday by the President, I believe we must read what he said into this bill. Mind you, I am not objecting to a reasonable amount of cooperation; but we must still remember that we are part of the British empire. While I am opposed to a complete programme of internationalism, I still favour it to a degree. In my view, internationalism should stay where it has always been, namely with Great Britain and her dominions, because that has been the only league of nations which has ever been successful in the history of the world. And why we should go outside it today, I do not know.
It was pointed out by my former leader only a few days ago that we have had no imperial conference. At that time he was referring to defence matters within the empire. When here in Ottawa, Mr. Curtin and Mr. Fraser, the prime ministers of two of our sister dominions which are now being seriously threatened so far as their security within the British empire and the world is concerned, are showing considerable interest in this matter.
I urge that this should have first been considered in an empire conference. The other prime ministers I named would have liked a conference in which Canada would join, but Canada rejected it. We now see the result of it in the statement made to the house by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) on Monday last. The question was raised by me of the announcement by Mr. Bevin on May 16 in London as to giving up our British bases in the Mediterranean, Suez and the middle east, abandoning that whole area, to retire to East Africa, unwept, unhonoured and unsung and the empire scuttled in this way, and Canada never heard of it. Where would we have been in the last war if we had given up all our bases?
Away back in 1939 some people right here in this house seemed to believe that we could depend upon Washington for all the defence we needed. It was said: Why do we want to go to London or to Glasgow for defence when we can get all the defence we want in Washington? If we had given up those bases; if we had not kept Hong Kong, Malta and the other great bases; if they had been given over to an international body, where would we have been during the last war? We would have had to be neutral, too. They said that we should go to Washington. The United States came into the war after it had been on for nearly two and a half years because they were invaded; Russia came into the war because she was invaded, but Great Britain went to war in the defence of Poland to which she had given a verbal agreement, afterwards a written agreement. Lord Bennett said:
We have not had an imperial conference for some time at which all of the commonwealth was represented and we have no parliament which speaks for all. We, therefore, are developing separate policies in the various nations of the commonwealth and you cannot have a commonwealth last long if all the nations that comprise it are developing separate policies.
What we are facing is the greatest crisis this country has ever faced-and the epitaph has been written in cold-blooded terms just as accurately as far as guessing can be accurate. Many countries believe we are through.

In my opinion we should have called a dominion conference on the principles of this bill.
I do not believe in Bill No. 253. I do not believe in the present methods adopted by the united nations. They have given us very little satisfaction. Even Mr. Attlee said he was disappointed in their first year. I believe that what is going on in New York now will lead to untold disaster for the people of this country if we depend upon that agency alone as we did upon the old league of nations before. I further believe, as to this bill, in the words of Mr. Churchill, who said:
I have never conceived that a fraternal association with the United States would militate in any way against the unity of the British commonwealth and empire, or breed ill-feeling with our great Russian ally, to whom we are bound by the twenty years treaty. I do not think we need choose this or that. With wisdom, and patience, and vigour, and courage, we may get the best of both. We have often said of our own British empire: "In my father's house there are many mansions."
That is correct. This bill and the provisions contained in it should first have been considered by the dominions at a meeting, like they used to have every few years to solve these dominion questions of trade, defence and migration.
Russia was referred to today by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdon-nell). I believe that the western democracies should speak out plainly as to what they believe. Unless there is a united effort by Russia and the senior members of the democracies, the United States and Britain, to come to an agreement, there will be, as that great president, Franklin D. Roosevelt, said, a war of survival. If another war comes, it will be a war of survival. It certainly will be a war of survival for the western democracies. The only way in which it can be stopped is to make it plain to the other great nations that we want their help in order that there may be peace on earth and good will toward men for all time, and the time is now to oppose the aims of Russia for world supremacy.
Under this bill it is proposed to have the armed forces of another country here in Canada. In view of what has been said, I think we should have the advice of our military advisers. What is the necessity of having those armed forces here at the present time? They can do no good. They are proposing to send a large Canadian army to the United States to train. It is true that in the last war the Royal Air Force had bases down south, in Mexico, but that is another matter.
Bill No. 253 must be considered along with another matter, the giving up of bases along the Atlantic from Newfoundland to British

Guiana. These have been given to the United States under a 99-year lease, which is practically a freehold, as any lawyer will tell you. That lease should be cancelled, and its cost charged to lease-lend by the United States. Now they are coming on to the land. Are we to have these forces come here? I wonder if the matter was taken up at Washington. I referred to this matter in another debate on civil aviation in 1944 when it was proposed to give up certain bases to an international body. After all is said and done, our history books will have to be rewritten if what is going on now is correct. It is said now that we owe nothing to history; that everything is internationalism; that we owe nothing to patriotism and all that kind of thing, and that Britain and the dominions come second to internationalism. If this goes on we shall have to revise our. history books. The same complaint has been made about the histories in the United States and in Canada. We are being asked to give up some of our sovereign rights and to change our status. We are being asked to give away these rights, and I am not referring only to the United States now.
I say: Let them use the bases and give them the raw materials up to our capacity to give, but give them bases by sovereignty-no. If we had given them away before we would have lost the last war. We would never have been in the last war. If we had an international policy in connection with the giving up of parts of the empire-bases-if we had given them up, where would we be today? As the Prime Minister said:
The Canadian government strongly favours a policy of international collaboration and cooperation in air transport and is prepared to support in international negotiations whatever international air transport policy can be demonstrated as being best calculated to serve not only the immediate national interests of Canada but also our overriding interest in the establishment of an international order which will prevent the outbreak of another world war.
I then went on to say what would apply also to Bill No. 253, that we should be ready to cooperate with our allies. I said we should allow them to use our air bases, but we should not give away sovereignty over them. The empire has thrown back its enemies from without and in my opinion she will go on to destroy them. Now is the time that we should try to recapture the spirit of empire and our faith and pride in our dominions and in our trade and commerce. The empire is a living thing and should not be allowed to go by default or into liquidation. The mother country and the dominions fought this battle alone for two years. Our soldiers carried on with those from India, New Zealand. South Africa, Australia and the

Visiting Forces
empire training plan. We stood shoulder to shoulder in the snows of Labrador and Newfoundland and in the heat of India and the far east.
In the days before the war you could go into any large port and find fifteen or sixteen ships from different parts of the empire carrying on their trade. I believe that this same spirit of empire cooperation will continue in the years that are to come. Canada should be ready to go along with the dominions and the empire. The time has come when the government should tell this house and the country what our relations are with the other sister dominions who fought alon-g with us for two years to save civilization. One of our great allies stood aside for over two years with Germany, but Russia has since made a glorious record in the last two years of the w'ar with Germany.
That is the speech I made in 1944, before the war was concluded. I was referring to the policy which should be adopted then'- this would apply also to this bill-in connection with the use of bases and having forces in the countrj'. In view of the Prime Minister's statement on February 12 last, I have yet to hear any real reason given for permitting troops of another country to be in Canada two years after the war.
One million men from the dominions went to the help of the mother country in the first world war and 130,000 of these men fell on the field of battle. These men went under their own status, autonomy and sovereignty, and what they did voluntarily changed the whole history of the world.
So far as this bill goes, I have my own views in connection with it. It simply comes down to this: Are we or are we not to continue to be a partner with the mother country in the defence of the empire and the world? We were her partner in two great wars, and the result was that the axis parties were defeated. In my opinion you are going to have wars until you change the hearts of men, and instead of sending delegates all over the world to leagues and the UNO-and we are sending them all over the seven seas now- we should be sending out missionaries to them to change the hearts of men. Without that, war is never far off. I have already quoted in the house the exact words of Premier Attlee of Great Britain in calling the attention of the country to the present danger of war.
Civilizations arise and continue to exist- and all history is the witness to the truth-when conditions are hard, only when
they are continually threatened, only when they are determined to maintain and defend their rule. They decline and fall when the external pressure is removed, or the inner spirit decays. The surrender may disguise itself in many forms, of which humanitarian sentiment is one. F. S. Oliver wrote:
If a country will not stand up for its rights, it must surely lose them. The spirit of giving in is the most fatal disease to which nations are subject, and it is apt to attack them, like a cancer, when they have arrived at the meridian.
As W. MacNeil Dixon says, in "The Human Situation":
When England's day comes to an end the principles which have contributed to its coming, Christian, pacifist, or whatever they may be styled, will not thereby be strengthened. On the contrary, such is the irony which pervades things human, they will have brought about their own eclipse, their own dissolution, and all the triumph of the opposing principles. The decline and fall of England, which will rejoice her enemies, will not be England's decline and fall only, but of all for which she stood, and not till then shall we know the extent of our miseries. I. at least, am not of the opinion that humanity, justice, freedom or Christianity, will be gainers in that fall.
Next to the Christian faith no other agency has done so much for freedom, liberty and civilization as the mother country has done with the aid of the dominions. It has stood like the Rock of Ages. We should study the history of the empire and! learn what it has stood for in the way of defence. Do not forget that if the dominions do not hang together they will hang separately, as none is able to go it alone, and the mother country will become a small empire like a second Denmark on the edge of Europe. Quebec would have been invaded in the last war and so would Ontario and the maritime provinces if Britain had not extended her help to us in Canada by the fleet. This country went to the aid of Britain and France in the first great w'ar, and tens of thousands of our young men from the province of Quebec and other provinces lie buried in France until the resurrection morn.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most speakers who have taken part in this debate have agreed that if United States forces are to come into this country a bill such as this to provide for their discipline and) internal administration is necessary. The main argument has revolved around the much wider question of the defence of Canada and, related to that, question, whether we should admit United States forces to this country and to what extent, if they are admitted, that would infringe upon our sovereignty. So far as these latter questions are
Visiting Forces

concerned, we must take a practical and realistic view. I think we are all agreed that we would like Canada to reach the theoretically perfect position of being able to look after our own defence entirely by ourselves, but the plain fact is that we have not one-quarter of the population which would be required to do that, so that in my view it is foolish to talk about it. Therefore we must depend upon the help of our natural friends and allies, the British empire and the United States.
There are a few members of this house who, judging from their remarks, do not believe in the united nations; but even they, I am sure, earnestly hope, as well as the rest of us, that the united nations will become an effective instrument to maintain world1 peace. At the present moment the fact is that it is not such an instrument and the prospects of its becoming such in the near future I think everyone will agree are not very good. Under such circumstances, it would in my opinion be absolute folly to rely on the united nations and not to take the best measures that are otherwise open to us for our own defence.
Our geographical position makes our defence and the defence of the United States one problem in these days. I think everybody who has looked into the question is convinced that any possible war which might break out will be waged, in the first instance at least, in the air, and the targets for that airborne attack will be the heavily industrialized areas of the northern part of the United States and the southern part of Canada. To win the war, the enemy would have to knock out that industrialized area and destroy our potential war-making capacity on this contintent. The areas, that is to say the land mass of Europe and Asia, from which any airborne attack could be launched, would send either planes, rockets or any other type of missiles against the targets I have indicated by the great circle routes passing over northern Canada. Those are just simple facts which practically everyone will admit. If that is so, it seems to me that the least we can do is to cooperate with the United States in setting up experimental stations in the north to devise, if it is possible to do so, a defence chain against a possible attack coming in over that area. Furthermore, I believe that a bill of this kind is necessary to enable us to do that; therefore I am in favour of it.
To me the whole situation stripped of what I would call probably the unessentials, comes down to this. Are we prepared to cooperate with the United States in the defence of this continent or not? The whole thing can boil down to that one question. To me it is
inconceivable that anyone should be opposed to such cooperation unless his sympathies lie with -the only possible aggressor at the present time. So far as I can see, the only possible aggressor for several years is Russia; or unless he is one who is desirous of introducing into this country a system of government and an economy which is similar to that practised in Russia. Apart from people of that kind, I find it inconceivable that anyone would oppose the idea of cooperation with the United States in the defence of this continent.
The people who appear to be afraid of this bill are allowing their desire for peace and for a successful united nations completely to obscure the realities of the position in which we are and in which the whole world is at the present time.
The attitude of the C.C.F., as exemplified by the speakers who have taken part in this debate seems to me to be essentially a return to the attitude adopted by the-m in the ten years prior to the outbreak of the war just concluded. It seems to me that their outlook on questions of this kind is exactly the same as that of many friends of mine in Calgary. In the period before the war, these people were all members of the -pacifist league and of this, that and the other thing. They advocated constantly that we should take no steps in the matter of military preparedness. I have had many of these people speak to me in a condescending and sneering way. They wondered why I was such a fool as to devote part of m-y time to militia training during the period. They seemed to insinuate that my intelligence was of a comparatively low order because I was wasting my time in such a way and held the view that another war might come and that we should prepare for it. As I say, I am afraid-and it alarms me-that the attitude of the C.C.F. at present is a return to that attitude. If that is so, it behooves all the rest of us to make sure that that attitude does not come in to anything like such widespread favour as it had in the period between the two wars, and result in our becoming so weak that another war would be brought on.
This afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, "If you accept the possibility that there may be another war, then this bill may be sensible". If I have not quoted him correctly I am sure he will correct me.

That is where our living begins; from there it expands, we hope, in friendship. We have tried to keep peace in our own family circles and communities, and I wish it could be done all over the world. I suggest for the consideration of the hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) that if we could bring the ideals of our families into the whole
world of nations we would accomplish a great deal. I know it is not easy, but it is worth trying. Anything that is good is worth trying. It is no use saying it is impossible until every avenue has been explored. It is far better to approach your neighbour or anyone with whom you are dealing by trying to discover the things on .which you can agree, than by trying to find the things upon which you disagree. I believe that is a good policy, a good philosophy; and if I were not a poor human sinner I would always try to carry it out.
I am going to say, in all honesty, that I do not see the necessity for this legislation, unless there is behind it some reason which I do not appreciate. If that should be the case it is all the more reason why I should support the motion to have it sent to a committee, where we can get the answers to these questions. As I say, if there is no move behind it, the act itself is not necessary. As a little boy I played around Halifax harbour; that was a long time ago. The. suggestion has been made by some who profess to look into the future, that the United States and Russia will likely be the antagonists in the next war and that Canada will be the battleground. I will admit that is a possibility. Anything is a possibility in this world that we live in, and always has been. But it is not inevitable that that will happen. It is not inevitable, on the checkerboard of politics in the international field, that finally these two tremendously strong nations will not find a way of resolving their differences. It is not even inevitable, if they do fight, that we have to be the battleground, although I will admit that is a strong possibility. But if we have to be the battleground, I should prefer Canada to be the battleground on one of two conditions. The first would be that we decide we would take no active part; we would declare ourselves neutral-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this cross-fire with regard to looking into the records, back history and so on is all very well, but I expect that if we read all through the records of Hansard we should find a great many inconsistencies. Right from the beginning of my remarks, I have tried to refrain from party political recriminations against any individual or group in the house. I did that for the simple reason that I started out by saying that 1 am a humble and patriotic citizen of Canada. While I am prepared to fight any political group in this house on the political hustings on matters that concern us in a political way, this particular issue seems to me to be large enough to be able to command the support, if I am correct, of anybody with any political views who feels the same way as I do about Canada.
There is another thing that I wish to point out, dealing with this matter of war between the two nations which have been mentioned. I have heard fairly strong groups in Canada at times claim that Canada has gone to war at the behest of the United Kingdom government, that we were not independent, that when Britain declared war we were automatically at war. I have heard that claim criticized severely and vocally and, I think, sincerely by the people who indulged in the criticism. Since the Statute of Westminster, we have always claimed that -we had complete freedom in that regard, and that we do not have to do that. I would hate to see something happen which would put us in the position of having to go to war at the behest

Visiting Forces
of another nation, no matter which one it was, if we claim we do not necessarily have to follow the lead of Britain. But even if we did, let me draw this to the attention of the house, that the British people have a twenty-year peace pact with the Soviet Union. If we are a full-fledged and cooperative partner in the British commonwealth of nations, while we do not have to join any peace pact Britain happens to join, I think we should respect it. And if we are going to respect it, we should do nothing which might in any way arouse suspicion against us on the part of a nation with whom Great Britain at the present time has that twenty-year peace pact.
Let us see how this works out. I want to refer to the united nations, because I believe this whole thing is a part of that great organization which we are trying to build. The hon. member for Temiscouata has said it has no value, and I have heard other members say the same thing. I cannot prove that it has. But I suppose we are to have a united nations organization of some kind or another. We may be united as were Joe Louis and Billy Conn when they came together in conflict; when they were united only for a time. Or we may have peaceful relations. But it is likely that we shall have a united nations organization of one kind or another; and I prefer the peaceful kind.
At the present time the united nations may fall short of the glory of God. .But the fact remains that if we are to hope for the kind of cooperation and international understanding which I believe everyone here would like to have, regardless of their words, their thoughts or their expectations-and I believe all of us hope sincerely that we may have that-then we must realize that we need some kind of organization. The united nations is one way of trying to set up machinery which will make it possible to bring about that purpose.
Hon. members have heard me speak about cooperative enterprise before in the house; I believe in it. I believe in it, whether it is cooperation commercially, municipally or in local school districts. No matter where it is, it is cooperation. Like the hon. member for Temiscouata, I believe in our family homes, and that in those homes we want peace and1 harmony, comfort, well being, good will and affection. We want to have those families run as we in those families believe they should be run. We want no other families coming in to tell us how to handle our family affairs, and we have no right to go into other families and tell them how to handle theirs.
But when the two families meet on common ground, where there must be a sidewalk
or a road, then they must get together and agree, if they are both going to use community enterprise. They must agree, if they are to take the same responsibilities as to where and how these things shall be built, and what they will be used for. That applies to school districts, to municipalities, to provinces, to the dominion, and it applies to relations between nations which go to make up a commonwealth such as the British commonwealth of nations. And this goes through to the rest of the world, if we are to have peace and harmony in the united nations.
Because of that, I must pin some faith in the united nations, because if we do not have that, then we have the other kind of unity, the kind where tremendous bodies are locked in warfare. And let me point this out, that if we choose that road-and I do not think we shall do so deliberately-but if we choose it ill-advisedly, then we shall subject our children and our grandchildren to unbelievable horrors.
I have helped bury the dead, I would remind the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness). I have seen men die around me. I have been through some of those conflicts, as have other hon. members in the house. Indeed, I believe all groups are well represented in that respect. I d'o not want to see that happen again. But if the new weapons we are told about are even a quarter as powerful as it is said they are, then what we have seen before will be only a tea-party compared with what the magnitude of another war might be. Because of that, I believe we should be most careful in doing anything at all in the parliament of this country which might possibly fan the fires and flames of suspicion which are already too greatly extended across the world at the present time.
I have said1 these things earnestly and honestly, sincerely believing that I am right in what I have said. And I do wish hon. members would send this bill to a committee until we can get every bit of information with respect to it. If it can be proven to me that this is a better and a necessary thing to do, more necessary than anything we have done before, then I shall withdraw my opposition to it, and gladly. But I should like to know the complete story.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak in this debate; but, since it began, several thoughts have passed through my mind.
I am not going to oppose sending the bill to the appropriate committee, because if it goes' there witnesses can be called and the whole matter investigated from every angle.
Visiting Forces

Hon. members will not be deterred from further discussion when the bill returns from committee. But in connection with the bill, and] with respect to what has been said in the last two days, let me say we must face the fact that we live in a most unsettled world. When I say that I am not for one moment saying that any nation in the world wants war. I do not believe any nation today wants war for the simple purpose of having war; and I am not accusing any nation of any such intention.
But it must be recognized and. we must face the reality that we do live in an unsettled world and, to my mind, it is the height of common sense for governments to care for the defence of their country. All countries do it, and it is the height of common sense for this government to care for the defence of Canada. When one speaks about defence he should not be branded as a warmonger. It is only common sense to lock one's door at night. It is the height of foolishness for one to say, "I am going to lock my door tonight, but I hope, it will not aggravate my enemy. I realize there may be some, enemies lurking around. There may be some who have an eye on my possessions. There may be others who for some reason or another do not like me. Perhaps I should leave my door open tonight, in case, by locking it, I aggravate my friends." People do not talk in that way and, as far as I am concerned, when it comes to national defence we have to look at the matter just as realistically as that.
I would suggest that the present government have a little larger picture and conception of things as they exist in the world than we, though we be members of parliament, could ever hope to have. I am not saying that we should not feel perfectly free to express ourselves on any matters relating to defence, but I think we have to recognize that when it comes to matters of defence, obviously everything is not exposed to the whole world. There are things that go on behind the scenes. There are negotiations and exchanges of information between one country and another. No doubt the present government which sits opposite have exchanged views with other countries, and I fancy the reason they are proposing this measure is based largely upon information they have received or conclusions they may have arrived at because of the exchange of views.
The hon. member who preceded me referred to the twenty-year pact between Great Britain and Russia. I think that is a commendable thing. I should hope that we would have no
trouble, not only for the next twenty years or fifty years, but perhaps for the next 100 years, or indefinitely. Even though there is a pact between those two great nations, let us remember that the British government have put in a more rigid form of conscription. In so doing, surely they considered whether such a step would render negotiations of the united nations less effective. Yet that government being a government very similar to hon. members to my right in its objectives, saw fit to take rather more adequate measures with respect to their defences. I say this with the utmost care. Surely a government should not be criticized when they show a desire to protect our interests, especially when they are right on the field, perhaps having their hands more upon the pulse of world situation than ours are.
I do not wish to be presumptuous, nor do I wish to sound a note of suspicion; but, as I said at the commencement of my remarks, all is not well. History records that sometimes agreements become scraps of paper. I hope that will not happen, but sometimes it does. In the light of that, it seems to me that' the nations of the world should arrive at a particular definition as to what an aggressor nation really is. How are we to describe an aggressor nation? How are we to know when some nation makes a move that can be termed "aggressive"? It seems to me that that is a question which should be settled in some way or another. I should like to put on the record a definition of "aggressor" which was proposed some years ago by Mr. Litvinov, at that time soviet commissar for foreign affairs, and adopted by representatives of the Soviet Union, Roumania, Estonia, Latvia, Poland, Turkey, Iran and Afghanistan, meeting in London at the convention for the definition of "aggression" on July 3, 1933. The definition runs as follows:
. . . The aggressor in an international conflict shall ... be considered to be that state which is the first to commit any of the following actions:
1.	Declaration of war upon another state;
2.	Invasion by its armed forces, with or without a declaration of war, of the territory of another state;
3.	Attack by its land, naval or air forces, with or without a declaration of war, on the territory, vessels or aircraft of another state;
4.	Naval blockade of the coasts or ports of another state;
5.	Provision of support to armed bands formed in its territory which have invaded the territory of another state or refusal, notwithstanding the request of the invaded states, to take in its own territory all the measures in its power to deprive those bands of all assistance or protection.

No political, military, economic or other consideration may serve as an excuse or justification for the aggression referred to . . .

Mr. Speaker, I rise after listening to this debate to express my support of the motion to refer the bill to a committee. I shall make a few comments and express a few ideas in connection with this bill which has provoked a most fortunate and interesting discussion. I say most fortunate because, while the bill at first sight appears somewhat unimportant and technical, its implications are very wide under world conditions today.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the excellent opening speech by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe) and to the factual presentation of his argument by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), and I appreciated very much the, shall I say, moderate and wise remarks of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) as well as a great deal of what the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) had to say. So far as this debate is concerned, there can be no question that this side of the house has made the most constructive contribution to the discussion.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), in replying last night, said that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) gave his statement to the house no opposition was expressed in the house and none in the country. I think that is quite correct, but when the Prime Minister reads a statement to the house we have no opportunity to reply
and express our opinions. So far as the country is concerned, the minister's statement is quite correct. But I think the minister will realize that the great majority of the members of this house, on reading the Prime Minister's statement, were under the impression that only a few technical personnel were being considered. Yet in this discussion the hon. member for Vancouver South has suggested that, possibly a division of United States troops might be brought into this country, and we heard no denial or protest from the Minister of National Defence or from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent).
Since the Prime Minister made his statement, there has been a change of foreign policy in the United States. The Truman foreign policy is now in effect. That is why I maintain that, while the mechanical features of this bill may seem unimportant and routine, the attitude of many people to the Prime Minister's statement regarding collaboration with the United States in defence has changed to some extent.
I wish to support strongly the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I shall not repeat them, but I think he presented a logical and valid argument in connection with this bill and for its reference to the committee. I want to support whole-heartedly his urging upon the government to do everything possible at this time to show our strong support for collective security and the principles of the united nations.
Personally I deplore the tendency on the part of some hon. members who have spoken in this debate of two great power groups in the world, the U.S.S.R. and the United States, to underestimate as it were the strength of the British commonwealth of nations. In the first place, I urge upon this government to do everything possible to avoid any public appearance of departure from support of the united nations. In addition, because of our membership in the British commonwealth of nations and because of our geographical position, I urge that we stand shoulder to shoulder in these matters with the other members of the commonwealth, because while Great Britain is in financial difficulties at the present time and the influence of the British commonwealth of nations may appear to be somewhat lessened, I have so much confidence in the balance and stability and traditions and in the future of the British commonwealth of nations that if peace is to be maintained in this world in the future I believe that it will be done as a result of the balanced stability, influence and moral character of the people of the British commonwealtl of nations. I urge,
Visiting Forces

Mr. Speaker, that Canada take a strong hand in that connection and not allow herself, even by implication, to be included in one power bloc or the other. In these difficult times there are so many people who see everything in black or in white, who are prejudiced, whose opinions are fixed. May I say that it is not a question of peace or victory; it is a question of peace or disaster. The last war has shown that there can be no victor, except in a military sense, in modern war in this modern world. It is not peace or victory; it is peace or disaster. I urge that we do everything possible to back the united nations as a great balancing and useful force at this critical time.
I consider that the government has not been quite frank with the house. The replies of the minister to date have given us information that we did not have before. For instance, while many of us thought, and reasonably so, that the visiting United States forces would comprise a small number of technical men, we are now told that it is possible, without any consultation of parliament, for the commander in chief of the Canadian army to invite any number of troops into this country. I am sure that all hon. members are keen on the proper defence of this country. But we have to look at this question from every aspect, and because I believe that the members of this house and the people of this country should have an opportunity to obtain full information on the implications of this bill and its relationship to the international situation today I intend to support the motion to refer the bill to a committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I read this bill I do not consider it one on which this house should divide on party lines. First, who sponsors the bill? The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent). In that he doubtless cooperates and collaborates with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton); and, knowing both of these men, is there anyone in this house who for a moment would say that they would support legislation in this House of Commons detracting from the best interests of the Dominion of Canada or do anything that would lessen our pride in Canada of which we are all so proud? I, for one, cannot bring myself to think that of them.
During this debate I have heard so many straw men built up and then knocked down by brave volleys of words, straw men with nothing of reality to them but wonderful to talk about and wonderful to attack gravely.
We have to face the fact that this Dominion of Canada is greater in area than the United States of America, and also that we

have a population of probably less than 12,000,000 people, whereas the United States has a population of some 130,000,000, and in our population of 12,000,000 there is a majority of women and children. So who are we to defend such a vast area successfully under modern methods of warfare? In our time the method of warfare has completely changed. As I grew up from childhood to young manhood, to manhood, I, like everyone else in this house, complacently felt that we were defended by the British navy and the British army; that we Canadians did not need to raise a hand to defend ourselves. It is true that that we sent a contingent to the South African war, but what did that mean in the long run in that war? The Canadians deported themselves well. They have done it in two great world wars, but alone we could not have had very much effect on the result of either of those wars. I think we are fortunate to be on the friendly terms that we are with the powerfully great nation bordering on our southern border. It is reasonable, it is sensible that Canada and the United States should cooperate in matters of defence and, if necessary, in matters of offence. We should exchange ideas as to defence, ideas as to attack and ideas as to armament.
WThat happened in the last war? Two big nations, dictator nations, Germany and Italy, undertook to conquer the democratic world. The British empire and commonwealth of nations took on the defence of the small nations that had been attacked by the dictatorship of Germany. The British commonwealth of nations consisting of Great Britain, the dominions of Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, India and Newfoundland, with France and the great United States of America saved democracy from dictatorship. But during that war the attacking dictators attacked another dictatorship, Russia. Who saved that dictatorship? The same democratic nations. If they had not stepped in and gone to Russia's defence Germany would have defeated Russia just as surely as we are here tonight. And the democracies of the world got little credit for it. It is no surprise that the democratic nations sitting at the peace table with a nation of dictators are having trouble arriving at a just peace. But I hope that they will overcome these difficulties successfully as they have in the past.
When that dictator nation was attacked by the attacking dictator nations that were fighting against us as democracies, what happened here in Canada? An element that up to that time was doing all it could to impede and injure Canada in the war, sud-

Visiting Forces
denly, overnight, became ultra loyal and wanted to see the democracies win. Why? Not because of their admiration or love or loyalty to Canada, but because of their comrades over in Russia. The communists, the so-called Labour Progressive party, were more concerned about the fate of Russia than of Canada.
I am particularly impressed and pleased with the provisions of section 4 of the bill. Although we are not in committee of the whole considering the bill section by section, we are considering the principle, and in my opinion this is one of the chief principles in it.
Nothing in section 3 of this act shall affect the jurisdiction of any civil court in Canada to try a member of a United States force for any act or omission constituting an offence against any law in force in Canada whether or not proceedings with respect to such act or omission have been instituted by a United States service authority or before a United States service court.
That is as it should be. In the war that so recently came to an end, we had a large force of the United States army come into Canada to carry out war measures, to build the Alaska highway, to tap our oil wells on the Mackenzie river and pipe them across to a refinery which they built in Yukon territory. The government of Canada, by an agreement with the government of the United States, sold the rights of Canadian civilians down the river. Canadian civilians injured, damaged or attacked by United States soldiers could not take them to a Canadian court. If they suffered an injury they had to take the award of a workmen's compensation board sitting where-in Canada? No, down in the state of New Jersey. They had to take it and like it. And if a United States soldier by his carelessness-and there were many instances of it-severely injured a Canadian civilian, committed property damage or personal damage, the Canadian citizen could not take it to court. He had to put up with what the United States army chose to give him. In one case a Canadian civilian driving his own truck lawfully, conforming with the rules of the road, was crashed into by a United States truck driven by a United States soldier. The Canadian truck was damaged so that it became utterly useless. The Canadian driver was injured. Both of his feet were , driven down through the floor of his truck; his leg was broken in two places above the knee; his pelvis was broken; his spine was injured and he will be a cripple for life. They had to cut the steering wheel with a hacksaw to get him out of the truck. The United States army offered to pay for the truck, the hospital and doctor bills. '1'hey have now 83166-246
consented to give him perhaps the munificent sum of S8,000. They will give it if the United States congress is good enough to vote the money, and not otherwise. If these conditions are prevented by this section of the bill I would support it, if for no other reason.
I could go on and tell of other instances that happened during, as they called it, the American occupation. When called upon the telephone, they would say "The American army of occupation speaking." That happened here in Canada. For my part, I say that this is a proper, useful and necessary legislation for this Canadian parliament to pass and I propose to support it.
