Personally I have no great objection to sending Bill No. 253 to the external affairs committee, but I think a good purpose has been served by allowing a number of hon. members to speak on this measure. I believe that the speeches which have been delivered so far are a fair indication of the views of hon. members on this important subject.
Many critics of the bill seem to be possessed with the idea that Canada is going to declare war on some nation in the near future, when in reality such is not the fact. Some hon. members criticized the bill, and they have said repeatedly that they did so because they want peace in this world. Well, who does not? By passing this bill, would we run the risk of getting into a war sooner than we would if the bill did not pass this house? I am not at all surprised that some hon. members should hold definite views in opposition to this bill, but I must admit that I was surprised to hear strange ideas expressed by several hon. members who are usually reliable in their thinking. One hon. gentleman stated that we should refuse to tolerate the idea that war is coming. I am sure all hon. members agree that no one in Canada wants war, and that perhaps no one in any other nation wants war. But surely that hon. gentleman must agree that, even if there is no likelihood of war, it is better for our people to be on guard than to tell them there will be no war and have them unprepared, as they were in 1939. Really I cannot understand how a responsible individual could believe that it is in Canada's interests to tell our people there will be no war-even though he does not know any more about it than I do-rather than to warn them of the possibil-[DOT] ity. I subscribe to the view that we should be on guard at all times; I think that is a good policy.
While I am on this point, I should like to mention one other matter. During the Easter recess, while I was on my way out west, .1

Visiting Forces

was a guest of a friend of mine who also invited a number of Canadians holding prominent positions. These men of learning began to discuss the question of defence, and one expressed the fear that Canada might provoke war. So he appealed to me and others to do everything within our power to see that the secrets of atomic energy were handed over to our "friends". He stated that he had formed his opinion on -that subject following a certain lecture by a prominent physicist at one of our universities, who told him that now this question was so serious that the Canadian people must do something about it. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members should take advice in military matters from military men. It is not enough for one to rise in his place and pretend to know everything about everything. This is not a small political issue. This is not a by-election. This is a serious matter, concerning the future of this nation. Surely we should have enough faith in our military men to take -their advice in matters of this kind and not assume that we have a knowledge and depth of understanding concerning these problems greater than anyone else.
Would anyone suggest, that- in the event of a war it would not be in Canada's interests to stand together with our neighbour? Would anyone suggest that it would be a good policy for Canada to stand idly by and await developments? I should like to ask hon. gentlemen who have been criticizing this measure and have expressed opposition to it to telll this house and the country whether they feel that Canada would be justified in taking the course they are advocating, if we were attacked in a surprise-war, and had not made preparations together with the United States in regard to defence. Surely they could not say that. Yet now they are trying to convince this house that it is not in Canada's interest to cooperate with the United States.
I am not of Anglo-Saxon origin, -but I do not believe any hon. member in this house is more pro-British than I am. In diplomatic affairs I believe the United Kingdom still leads the world-; I am frank in making that statement. In economic and monetary matters it is true the United States has taken over the lead; but the United States has still a great deal to learn when it comes to matters having to do with various European countries, and world diplomacy. The British have had a great deal of experience in these matters, and of course experience counts. At the same time I maintain that- it is in our interests to cooperate with the United States in order that we may arrange our hemispheric defence
[Mr. Hlynka.l
programmes. We did that during the war, * and why should we not have this understanding with our good neighbour to the south during peace time?
Some may say this is peace time, and as a matter of fact some hon. members have stated that they would not object to our entering into this understanding with the United States if this were a time of war, but they are opposed to it now because this is peace time. What a shallow argument! I maintain that the war which began in 1914 was not concluded, and that it continued. We say a war breaks out, but that is not so; it is peace that breaks out now and then. From 1914 to 1918 we had a period of military warfare. Then there was a breathing spell. The struggle continued again from 1939 to 1945, and today it is still continuing short of military warfare. The fight is going on every day in the councils of the united nations, in the press, over the radio, and so on. Let me just quote from a press dispatch which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of this morning, June 5, 1947:
Budapest, June 4-(AP)-Soviet Lt.-Gen. V. P. Sviridov has refused permission for an American officer to inspect military installations of Hungary, a former enemy country, American spokesmen disclosed today. The soviet action raised speculation that the Russians may already be taking a hand in training the Hungarian army.
Then farther down in the article:
American spokesmen said Colonel _ John _ H. Stokes. Jr., of San Francisco, executive officer of the United States military mission asked War Minister Lajos Dinnyes, now the new procommunist premier, for permission to inspect a Hungarian division. Ordinarily such a request would be a mere formality in view of relations between a victor power and a defeated former enemy.

They have been the strongest advocates of surrendering Canada's sovereignty to some super power that they do not know and we do not know, a power that, to my knowledge has not done anything for Canada and has not shown any good result so far. Yet they keep on pleading with the people, and delivering speeches all across this country, telling the Canadian people that we must give up a part of our sovereignty. I should like to refer to the various international organizations. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the various international organizations which have been organized thus far have been, and are today, the instrument of internationalism and the vehicles of communism, however disguised. And they do it right along. Then, as my hon. friend the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) said, they waste time in pretending that we are getting somewhere. We are not. During the past few years too many of our leading men became obsessed with the so-called global philosophy. We have been hearing public men speaking about things on a global scale. And the bill applies exclusively to United States troops. So I refer to them, not with any suggestion that it is undesirable that United States troops be admitted, but merely because they are the only ones affected by the bill.
It is a new policy, in that Canada is now inviting United States troops into this country on a basis and under conditions which Canada has never extended to any other troops before in peace time. We should ask at the outset how many troops are here and how they came here. We should ask what exactly were the terms upon which they were admitted, for how long we expect them to stay, and if we expect any large increase in their number.
In the course of my remarks, which I intend shall be brief, I shall state why I think it is important that these questions be answered. I wish to refer to something the hon. member for Vancouver South said last night. Everybody in the house is agreed that it is essential that we should adopt any and every method which may lessen the possibility of another war. It seems to me that one of the factors making most directly for another war would be to have the world divided into two power blocs, because they cannot avoid coming into direct conflict at almost every stage. But if there were three or more groups of powers the danger of direct conflict would be that much further removed, because there would be three or more different pulls of interest. It is with that thought in the back of my mind that I say we should be careful to understand what we are doing, and we should be careful not to transfer entirely to the United States all the community of interest and collaboration which, under the traditional background of our policy and interests, have lain elsewhere.
There is one concrete suggestion I should like to put forward, and that is that it would be preferable if, instead of having a separate bill dealing with the United States, we passed an act in the form of their own Friendly Foreign Forces Act to which the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) referred last night, a general bill capable of extension to the troops of any country which Canada sees fit to admit to our own soil. Mr. GEORGES H. HEON (Argenteuil): Mr. Speaker, as I studied the bill before the house I was reminded of an article written in the January, 1946, issue of Foreign Affairs, under the signature of Lionel Gelber, entitled "Canada's New Stature". Mr. Gelber states:
In that momentous redistribution of world power now taking place, Canada must be classed with those nations which have gained rather than lost in stature. Her increased importance exemplifies the shift toward a system of international affairs founded on centres of authority removed from western and central Europe. For Canada has undergone a far-reaching diplomatic revolution. In some respects this is admitted and proclaimed by her leaders; in other respects it is concealed. Canada is one of the few countries among the united nations in which the prewar helmsmen of the ship of state are still at their posts. They are in fact steering a new course, but since they are loath to confess that their seamanship ever was at fault, they prefer to describe it merely as accelerated progress along the old one. They can put it in such terms because external affairs are seldom major issues in Canadian politics and neither politicians nor officials have been judged in Canada, as elsewhere among the democracies, on their pre-war records.
But the evidence of Canada's new position in the world is unmistakable.
The bill before this house establishes a momentous precedent, the consequences of which no one at this moment can fully visualize. Bluntly, the bill means that there will be United States armed forces in undefined numbers on Canadian territory in peace time and that they will have their own military laws and courts. In theory this move is repugnant to our muoh vaunted sovereignty, and in this hour of internationalism I am very much afraid that further offences against sovereignty will be committed, as they have been openly and sometimes cruelly committed in the last few years. However, Canada must act according to her own situation in a changing world which has put her at the cross-roads of the Big Five.
No longer is Canada, as was stated at the Versailles treaty making, a fireproof house far away from incendiary materials.

Mr. Speaker, in this House of Commons we have sometimes been accused of speaking to the people back home. On this occasion I intend to speak to the House of Commons and to speak plainly to the people back home. I do not want the house to be in any doubt as to where I stand on this particular legislation. Before I touch upon that. I wish to make two observations about the world as it stands. As the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) said, in the last eighteen months or two years international relations have considerably worsened; in other words, since the San Francisco- conference. To me it is rather a harsh criticism of our civilization to think that today easily ninety-nine per cent of the people of the world are seeking nothing but peace; yet in the meantime we seem to be heading toward something quite different from- it.
A friend of mine once remarked-I am sure what he said is quite true-that if we could have some law enforceable, which of course we can not. that all future wars should
Visiting Forces

be fought by men over fifty years of age, we would have no more wars. That is a true statement of fact. But it lies with us older people to try to find a solution which will mean that our youngsters will not once more be subjected to what they have been in the last two wars. In these times of modern weapons, we fellows over fifty years of age will be in the picture, but only on the receiving end.
I wish to say a word about this bill. What I intend to say I shall put in a sentence or two. I am 100 per cent opposed to the amendment; I am 100 per cent in favour of the bill, and I shall so vote. There is no equivocation or anything of that sort in what I have said. Realistically our position is this. If we believe anything we read in the newspapers; if we discuss with persons who have gone from here to international organizations, then we can see that they are all worried. There is not any doubt about that.
We can talk as we like of ideals, and I agree with many of the idealistic things that have been said, but to be practical about the matter our position is this. I regard as highly as anyone the interest we have in our sovereignty; but, on the other hand, we are in this position. If a mouse is attacked by a cat it does not *worry much about sovereignty; it hopes that a terrier will come along and kill the cat. That is the position in which we are-let us admit it-with our tremendous boundary line. We are not in a position to defend it. Where are we to get help? In France which was mentioned, in China and in all these other places? I agree with what, so many people have said, that it is unthinkable among rational beings that war should come, but today international affairs are being, conducted, in the judgment of us who are sitting here and other ordinary people in the country, on a basis which we cannot conceive or believe to be rational. Therefore, stripping the tree of its branches and leaves and getting down to the bare trunk, to the basic position, it is this. If, which God forbid, war comes, where are we to look for help except to our friends in the United States of America? Where are we to look for practical help? It is no use theorizing about these things. That is the only place we can get help. May I say this to the right hon. gentleman who is piloting, the bill? I went over and spoke to him a moment ago and asked him about how many of these people were here and he said, about sixty. So far as I am conc'erned I hope they come in their thousands to help our defences to defend the country if we are attacked. We are not going to attack anybody. It is unthinkable. Nobody dreams that

we should; but let us defend ourselves with the weapons we have and with those which we can'get from a friendly people. I hope, sir, that I have left no doubt where I stand on this bill.

This bill is similar to the one which the United States forces had in the United Kingdom during the war and which was passed by the British parliament. Since I had an opportunity to observe the functioning of that bill with regard, to the jurisdiction of United States military courts over there personally, I found, and I think the general opinion was, that the bill worked extraordinarily well. It gave the United States courts and the United States courts martial the right to try their own personnel, and a wise right that was because the United States code of laws is considerably different from that in the United Kingdom. It had one thing which I think we have a little overlooked in this bill, namely, the prejudice that a civilian court has when trying a uniformed national of a friendly country. I would think that the civilian courts in Canada, and I am sure the civilian courts in England, welcomed' the fact that the delicate business of trying offenders against breaches of the law was taken out of their hands. I can see, and it is obvious that anybody who has had experience will know, the difficulty of a court of law passing sentence, against a member of an armed force that is serving as a friendly nation within the borders of his country.
We found that the civilian courts were, in many instances, loath to pass sentence or to try the offenders, in, some cases our own, Canadian soldiers because they were friendly people, and there was the difficulty of a court, particularly a jury, wishing to take action against a member of the visiting armed forces, because it might be construed as an unfriendly act. How fortunate it is that the United States has this clause in their general military set-up, that it is their practice that all these delicate situations are handled by themselves. The Canadian bill does not give the United States authorities power over our courts, which still may try United States service personnel for breaches of Canadian civil or criminal law, if the authorities are not satisfied, with the United States action.
That brings me to another point, namely, that this bill has nothing to do with sovereignty. How the question of sovereignty came in, I do not know; but it has nothing to do with it. This bill merely gives United States forces the right to try their own personnel.

Let us go on to the atomic energy commission; what happened there? The United States, Great Britain and other nations on that
commission offered a fair and workable plan. They offered to make their secrets known; they offered mutual inspection of the production of atomic energy all over the world. What happened? The proposal was thrown out of court by the Russian delegate, Gromyko, and an absolutely untenable position taken under which the Rusisans wished the Americans to give up all their science and knowledge in regard to atomic energy and destroy everything they had done, including the possibility that this new force might become one of the greatest benefits mankind has ever known. So we had an untenable position, frustration and obstruction by Russia.
Then let us see what happens every day in the Russian press and over the Russian radio. We get nothing but absolute vilification and abuse of the democracies. Is that the way in which a friendly power is likely to behave? The other day we saw the coup d'etat in Hungary. We see what has happened in Greece, in Albania, in Yugoslavia and in Poland. Everywhere we see Russian communist infiltration and hostile actions toward the democracies; the mining of the straits of Corfu ; getting the little Soviet satellites to commit overt acts; continuous unrest; subversive activity and hostility toward the major powers. Is that the way in which a peaceful nation is likely to act?
Then let us look at the troubles of the forces of occupation in Germany and Austria. Do we get cooperation between the United States, British and French zones and the Russian zone? We do not. Friends of mine on the control commission have told me that it is as much as their life is worth to go over the border of the Russian controlled zones, particularly in Germany. Do we see any effort on the part of Russia to try to rehabilitate Germany or Austria, without which there can be no economic peace in the world? No; we see them taking every bit of productive machinery out of the country. Is that likely to help the rehabilitation of Europe?
Then let us look at what has happened in our own country. Whether or not we like to admit it, today we are at war politically with Russia. Right in this very House of Commons we have seen that, but we forget these things. We have seen prominent, trusted civil servants subverted by Russian agents, right here in Canada. We have seen an attempt by soviet agents to grab the secrets of atomic energy. Was that a friendly act? Was that a friendly gesture between two nations? Then we see communist - controlled, communist - fostered strikes throughout the length and breadth of
Visiting Forces

Canada. I had one in my own riding, and I do not mind mentioning it. That was the Anaconda strike, which lasted for five months, during which every member of the union lost $1,000 in pay. Now it has been shown that the man behind that strike was Reeve Robinson, named as a strong communist in Newsweek. Then what else do we see? Is any member of this house fool enough to believe that communist activity in Canada is not controlled from Moscow?

Second, appeasement has always caused wars. If the hon. members who

have opposed this bill are so blind that they are now prepared to support any appeasement, then I want this house and this country to know it.
The next matter for consideration is this: Has the United States ever attacked anybody? Has Russia? I just leave those questions with the house.
The next matter for consideration is that we are not only geographically in the firing line, but are also the great storehouse and powerhouse of the world. As has been said, we cannot protect ourselves because our population is too small. We must face that. fact. We must have help.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the next war will be a push-button war. We shall not require big battalions. We shall not require divisions and army groups. The next war will be fought with the new weapons. We might just as well admit that now. All this bill seeks to do is to allow our great friend and neighbour, the United States, to help us put our pushbuttons in place, so that if we are attacked we can neutralize the attack before the new weapons take effect on our centres of population. I support this bill with all my heart and I am utterly and1 completely against the amendment.

I do not have to, but I want to say this before the bill is given second reading. I think most of the debate on this bill has been deplorable. This is a very simple bill, whether we agree with the principle or not. It is a bill to allow a foreign country, whose military forces are here by our invitation or consent, to set up their own courts to deal with infractions of the rules or the law. To hear speeches such as that made by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) just now, one would think this bill was the first step in a declaration of war. To me it is not understandable that reasonable men should say the things that were said by most of the members who have spoken in this debate.
The hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe) made what I thought was a reasonable speech. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), in my opinion, made an excellent speech in regard to this bill. I did not hear the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), but I am told that he also made a very good speech, as did the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. JUNE 5, 1947
Privilege
Merritt), and some of the other members. But for most of the debate today one would think this bill the first step in a war. The hon. member for York West did not leave any doubt about it. All of his speech was taken up with the danger of Russia, and he was in favour of this bill because it was the first step in stopping Russia, Surely that is not the way to build peace. Have my hon. friends to my right discarded the idea of the united nations' Are they going to throw away everything we have tried, with so much labour, to build since April, 1945? If they want to do that they had better say so and tell this country to go on an armed footing at once.
